Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Resilient Bayer stock as Japan clears Hyrnuo lung cancer drug - Ad-hoc-news.de
Drugs & Therapies.content:
Bayer AG (DE000BAY0017): Börsen-Editorial-Szene mit DAX-Handelssaal, großen Bildschirmen und abstrakten Pharma-Aktienkursen im Frankfurter Finanzviertel, Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Bayer AG (ISIN DE000BAY0017) stock eased modestly on August 24, 2026, even as the company reported a key regulatory win in Japan for its Hyrnuo targeted lung cancer therapy and continued to lean on improving second-quarter 2026 financials.
Per market data as of August 24, 2026, Bayer shares were recently quoted between 47.63 EUR and 47.79 EUR in European trading, down between 0.5 percent and 0.85 percent on the day, versus a last closing price of 48.04 EUR and with the year-to-date performance shown as a gain in the high-twenties percent range. Hyrnuo’s approval headlines in Japan appeared alongside this modest pullback, suggesting investors are weighing the new oncology asset against valuation and litigation considerations. Bayer’s latest quarterly report for Q2 2026 confirmed that Group sales grew 2.2 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis to €10.872 billion and EBITDA before special items rose 1.9 percent to €2.144 billion, giving investors an updated earnings base for assessing the stock.
Japan approves Hyrnuo for HER2 NSCLC
On August 24, 2026, Bayer announced that Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare had granted marketing approval for Hyrnuo, also known as sevabertinib, as a targeted therapy for patients with HER2 mutation-positive unresectable advanced or recurrent non-small cell lung cancer. The company’s communication highlighted that Hyrnuo is aimed at HER2 (ERBB2) mutation-positive disease in the non-small cell lung cancer setting, a segment of oncology where targeted therapies have reshaped standards of care. The regulatory decision in Japan follows Bayer’s development work in HER2-driven tumors and adds a new commercial opportunity for its Pharmaceuticals division in one of the largest healthcare markets outside the United States.
Same-day coverage of the Hyrnuo approval noted that Bayer shares on Tradegate were indicated at 47.66 EUR to 47.78 EUR around 11:39 a.m. local time on August 24, 2026, with the intraday change between negative 0.55 percent and negative 0.78 percent, while the stock’s year-to-date performance was cited at roughly plus 28.80 percent to plus 28.97 percent and an average analyst price target in the mid-50s EUR range. These figures place the current share price several euros below the cited average target, underlining that even after a strong run since the start of 2026 investors have not fully closed the gap to consensus valuation. At the same time, another intraday snapshot referenced a quote of 58.40 EUR with a daily decline of 0.82 percent and a last closing price of 58.88 EUR along with an average price target of 72.62 EUR, indicating that in some trading venues or instruments linked to Bayer the implied upside versus the mid-70s EUR target remains more pronounced.
For long-term shareholders, the Japanese approval of Hyrnuo serves as a tangible signal that Bayer’s Pharmaceuticals pipeline is delivering new assets at a time when the group continues to manage legacy litigation and a high net-debt load. The HER2-mutant non-small cell lung cancer indication is a focused niche compared with broad oncology markets, but targeted therapies in specific molecular subtypes can command premium pricing and support margins when they achieve strong uptake. Investors will watch subsequent launches, reimbursement decisions, and real-world data from Japanese patients to gauge whether Hyrnuo can materially contribute to Bayer’s pharmaceuticals growth trajectory beyond the initial regulatory milestone.
Q2 2026 earnings and guidance context
Bayer’s second-quarter 2026 results provide the current fundamental backdrop for the stock, with Group sales reported at €10.872 billion and an increase of 2.2 percent on a currency- and portfolio-adjusted basis. The company stated that EBITDA before special items in Q2 2026 rose 1.9 percent to €2.144 billion, underscoring that profitability grew slightly ahead of sales despite ongoing investments and litigation-related costs. Net income recovered to €219 million in the quarter from a year-earlier loss of €199 million, marking a swing of €418 million toward profitability and giving the group positive bottom-line momentum compared with the prior-year period.
Management also reported that core earnings per share in Q2 2026 came in at €0.95, which represented a 16.7 percent decline versus the prior-year quarter. The explanation pointed to tax normalization and reconciliation items rather than deterioration in underlying operations, suggesting that adjusted earnings quality remained intact even as the headline EPS metric faced pressure. Free cash flow was negative €371 million in the second quarter and negative €2.7 billion for the first half of 2026, with €2.5 billion of litigation payouts highlighted as a major driver of cash outflows. Net financial debt stood at €33.6 billion at the end of the period, and Bayer reiterated a full-year 2026 net-debt target range of €29 billion to €30 billion, supported in part by a €3 billion equity investment from Apollo and a $5 billion bond placement; this planned reduction of between €3.6 billion and €4.6 billion versus the Q2 level is central to the deleveraging narrative.
In addition to these figures, Bayer confirmed its full-year 2026 guidance in the Q2 2026 reporting, signaling that management sees no need to adjust its outlook despite the cash-flow drag from litigation and the mixed core EPS trend. For investors, the combination of modest top-line growth, improving net income, and firm guidance suggests a stabilizing operating environment, even if debt metrics and free cash flow remain key watchpoints. The Hyrnuo approval in Japan now slots into this context as a new potential contributor to future Pharmaceuticals sales, which in Q2 2026 were reported at €4.458 billion with EBITDA before special items in that segment at €1.055 billion, numbers that frame the scale of Bayer’s established prescription-drug franchise relative to new launches.
From a valuation perspective, the average price targets in the mid-50s EUR to low-70s EUR range cited in market-data coverage indicate that equity analysts see scope for further upside relative to spot quotes in the high-40s EUR and mid-50s EUR bands. The gap between current trading levels, such as 47.63 EUR to 47.79 EUR or 58.40 EUR to 58.88 EUR, and consensus targets underscores an ongoing debate about how quickly Bayer can turn its improving earnings trajectory into stronger free cash flow while containing litigation risk. If net debt trends toward the €29 billion to €30 billion target by year end and Hyrnuo plus other pipeline assets deliver visible revenue contributions, investors may be more prepared to assign higher multiples to the stock.
Hyrnuo strengthens Bayer’s oncology portfolio
Hyrnuo, or sevabertinib, adds a specialized lung cancer therapy to Bayer’s oncology product suite and targets HER2 mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancer that is unresectable, advanced, or recurrent. The Japanese approval described Hyrnuo as a targeted therapy focused on HER2 (ERBB2) mutation-positive disease, aligning with the industry’s shift toward precision medicine where treatments are tailored to molecular drivers rather than broad histologic categories. For Bayer’s Pharmaceuticals division, this indication extends its reach in thoracic oncology and complements other targeted agents in the portfolio.
Non-small cell lung cancer with HER2 mutations represents a subset of the overall NSCLC population, but these patients historically had limited targeted options compared with those whose tumors carried EGFR or ALK alterations. By bringing Hyrnuo to market in Japan, Bayer positions itself within this evolving treatment landscape and opens the door to potential combination strategies or label expansions as data accumulate. If the therapy demonstrates robust efficacy and manageable safety in real-world practice, it could help reinforce the perception that Bayer’s oncology pipeline is capable of generating differentiated assets beyond its traditional strengths in areas such as cardiovascular and women’s health.
Commercially, Japan is a significant contributor to global oncology revenues given its advanced healthcare system and willingness to reimburse innovative therapies that deliver meaningful patient benefits. The approval of Hyrnuo therefore not only validates Bayer’s clinical development in HER2-mutant NSCLC but also offers a concrete revenue opportunity that can support Pharmaceuticals segment growth over the coming years. The eventual impact on group-level numbers will depend on pricing levels, speed of uptake among oncologists, competition from other HER2-targeted agents, and the extent to which Bayer can secure regulatory approvals for Hyrnuo in additional regions such as Europe and North America.
Bayer stock and current trading context
On August 24, 2026, intraday market snapshots from European venues showed Bayer shares trading in the high-40s EUR range on Xetra and Tradegate, including prints at 48.01 EUR and 48.08 EUR in Xetra and indications at 47.63 EUR to 47.78 EUR in Tradegate, with daily changes between negative 0.08 percent and negative 0.85 percent. One set of data cited a last closing price of 48.04 EUR and a five-day change hovering slightly negative, while the year-to-date performance was listed at gains between 28.75 percent and 28.97 percent. Another snapshot referenced a 58.40 EUR intraday quote tied to a prior closing level of 58.88 EUR and a one-year change around negative 36 percent, reinforcing that Bayer-related securities can show differing price histories depending on venue and instrument, but the common thread is that the core German listing has delivered a strong rebound in 2026 after previous declines.
The contrast between the roughly plus-29 percent year-to-date performance on Xetra and the negative mid-30 percent one-year change in certain other data underscores how the measurement window can alter perceptions of the stock’s momentum. Investors focusing on 2026 alone see a company in recovery mode, supported by stabilizing operations, new product approvals such as Hyrnuo, and deleveraging measures including the €3 billion Apollo equity investment and $5 billion bond placement. Those looking back over a longer horizon still see the scars of past litigation and restructuring, with cumulative performance more subdued, and accordingly may demand clearer evidence that free cash flow and debt reduction targets can be achieved sustainably.
In practical terms, the combination of a current Xetra price around the 48 EUR mark and an average analyst price target in the mid-50s EUR band suggests potential upside of several euros if Bayer executes on its guidance and litigation management. When compared with the higher 72.62 EUR average target cited in another set of data, the implied upside from a 58.88 EUR last close is more limited in percentage terms but still meaningful. This quantifiable gap between spot prices and consensus targets is an important element of the investment case, and the Hyrnuo approval adds a fresh fundamental datapoint that could help close the gap if it translates into incremental revenue and profit over time.
As of the latest Q2 2026 figures, Bayer’s net financial debt of €33.6 billion remains substantial relative to its €10.872 billion quarterly sales base, highlighting why deleveraging is central to equity holders. The targeted reduction of net debt to the €29 billion to €30 billion range by year end implies an improvement of between €3.6 billion and €4.6 billion, a shift that would enhance balance-sheet resilience and potentially support a higher valuation multiple. The ongoing negative free cash flow, driven by €2.5 billion of litigation payouts in the first half, shows that the path to that target is not without risk, but the combination of external capital injections and operating cash generation could still move debt metrics in the desired direction if litigation cash flows moderate.
Crop protection collaboration enhances diversification
Beyond pharmaceuticals, Bayer’s strategy includes strengthening its crop protection and biologicals offerings, illustrated by a collaboration in biological crop protection where a partner announced on August 24, 2026, that it had received a first milestone payment under a license and collaboration agreement initially signed in December 2023 with Bayer AG. The statement described this payment as a milestone under a broader agreement focused on developing and commercializing biological crop protection technologies. For Bayer, such arrangements expand its pipeline of sustainable agricultural solutions that can complement traditional chemical crop protection and align with global efforts to reduce environmental impact while maintaining yields.
Biological crop protection typically involves using naturally derived or biologically based agents to manage pests and diseases, potentially reducing reliance on synthetic chemicals. By partnering with a specialist in this area and supporting development through milestone payments, Bayer positions its Crop Science division to participate in the growth of biologicals as regulators and farmers seek more sustainable solutions. The milestone payment reported on August 24, 2026, signals that development work under the collaboration has reached defined objectives and that the program is progressing toward potential commercial stages.
This diversification into biological crop protection complements Bayer’s efforts in pharmaceuticals and consumer health, giving the group exposure to multiple secular trends including precision oncology and sustainable agriculture. For investors, the collaboration highlights that even while litigation and debt management remain central challenges, Bayer is continuing to invest in future-oriented businesses that could support earnings and valuation in the medium to long term. The combination of Hyrnuo’s approval in Japan and progress in biological crop protection provides a multi-segment narrative that could appeal to shareholders who favor diversified health and agriculture exposure rather than a pure-play focus.
Closing view on Bayer shares
As of August 24, 2026, Bayer stock in its German listing was most recently quoted around 47.78 EUR on Tradegate, down 0.55 percent on the day, with a last closing price of 48.04 EUR and a year-to-date performance near plus 28.97 percent, while the latest Q2 2026 results showed Group sales of €10.872 billion and EBITDA before special items of €2.144 billion alongside net income of €219 million and a net-debt target of €29 billion to €30 billion for year end. The new Hyrnuo approval in Japan and ongoing collaborations in areas such as biological crop protection sit against this backdrop, offering additional fundamental angles for investors evaluating how much upside remains between current trading levels and consensus price targets.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Top Biopharma Analyst Sees Biotech M&A Market Reopening After a Long Freeze - 24/7 Wall St.
Pharma Industry.content:
Barclays’ Emily Field,
Head of U.S. Biopharma Equity Research,
told CNBC
on Monday, August 24, that
the biotech M&A freeze is over.
She sees capital markets reopening, large-cap pharma buyers committing to more deals, and fresh oncology data
proving that innovation extends well beyond weight-loss drugs.
Why Biotech M&A Suddenly Froze
Field described the prior slowdown in blunt terms.
“For a while we had
the GLP-1 story,
though it felt that that was very company-specific. And then at the beginning of the Trump administration, there were so many questions about broader policy, drug pricing. And so it felt like it put M&A, which really is the lifeblood of the biotech industry, kind of on pause for a while,”
she said.
She believes we’re at a turning point:
“We get to 2026, and it feels like the capital markets are open for a lot of biotech companies.
We’re starting to see more M&A from the large pharma buyers.
And then also some real innovation I think has really got markets excited. We had Revolution Medicines’
pancreatic cancer data
earlier this year. And then just last week, we saw the
Phase 3 results
for the cancer vaccine from Moderna and Merck,
“
Field said.
Cancer Vaccine Catalyst Behind the Call
Moderna
(
NASDAQ:MRNA
|
MRNA Price Prediction
) and
Merck
(
NYSE:MRK
) are co-developing intismeran autogene, a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine. Moderna’s CEO told investors the program is advancing across
“a broad portfolio of nine Phase II and Phase III studies,”
and that the Phase 3 study in adjuvant melanoma is fully enrolled. The five-year Phase 2b data at ASCO 2026 showed a 49% reduction in risk of recurrence or death with the vaccine plus KEYTRUDA versus KEYTRUDA alone, per Moderna’s
Q2 press release
.
The market reaction was immediate. Moderna jumped 177%, and Merck rose 12.5% on the readout covered by CNBC on August 20. Moderna shares are now at $145.04, up 392.13% year to date. Merck trades at $152.54, up 47.07% year to date, with Keytruda-family sales growing 4% to $8.4 billion in Q2.
Revolution Medicines Put Pancreatic Cancer Back in Focus
Revolution Medicines
(
NASDAQ:RVMD
) is the other data point Field highlighted. The RAS(ON) inhibitor developer’s RASolute 302 Phase 3 in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer showed median overall survival of 13.2 months versus 6.7 months for chemotherapy, with a hazard ratio of 0.40.
CEO Mark Goldsmith said the company has
“rapidly translated unprecedented Phase 3 results for daraxonrasib into an active Expanded Access Program and the filing of our first New Drug Application.”
Shares sit at $209.46, up 162.98% year to date, on a
$45 billion market cap
that keeps Revolution firmly on the industry’s oncology M&A radar.
Patent Cliffs Make More Acquisitions Inevitable
Field says expiring patents will make more acquisitions inevitable:
“The large-cap pharma companies have basically, even after having done deals, for example, AbbVie after the announcement of the deal earlier this summer, was very vocal that
they’re still committed to doing more business development.
Merck, even with the pipeline success that they’ve had on their own, has done a number of sizable deals,
has indicated that they’re still going to be very active,
“
she said.
AbbVie
(
NYSE:ABBV
) announced a
$10.9 billion acquisition
of
Apogee Therapeutics
expected to close in Q3 2026, and management said it has
“ample financial capacity for more business development.”
Merck’s Rob Davis called Keytruda’s coming loss-of-exclusivity
“more of a hill than a cliff,”
a comment underpinned by the Cidara ($9.0B), Terns ($5.8B), and Verona Pharma acquisitions.
The Catalysts That Could Keep the Boom Alive
Field’s closing point ties it together.
“These large pharma companies are just going to be
continuing to look at biotech to supplement their portfolios,
“
she said. Merck faces its Keytruda patent cliff. AbbVie is managing Humira erosion, with Q2 sales down 35.9% to $756 million. Both need
external innovation
to hit growth targets in the 2030s, and Field’s argument is that the market narrative has widened beyond GLP-1s to reward it.
Contact
[email protected]
for any questions or corrections.

Biopharma Equity Research,
on Monday, August 24, that
the biotech M&A freeze is over.

Pharma Industry.content:
China's innovative drug BD deals top $100 billion in H1; pharma valuation reset window opens
Add to Google Preferred Sources
China's innovative drug industry is at a critical juncture, transitioning from "fast-follow innovation" to "differentiated innovation." In the first half of 2026, China's innovative drug business development (BD) deal value totaled approximately $110 billion, already exceeding 80% of the full-year 2025 level, with deal structures upgrading to "platform-based BD." Companies including Hengrui Medicine, Fosun Pharma, Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals, and Huahai Pharmaceutical continue to ramp up R&D investment while pursuing differentiated global expansion strategies. Meanwhile, AI is reshaping the competitive landscape for global pharma, shifting core competitiveness toward proprietary knowledge bases and strategic decision-making capabilities. Although the SWS Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index has risen nearly 14% since the second half began, secondary-market valuations for innovative drugs remain conservative, with future cash flows from BD deals not yet fully incorporated into DCF models. Industry analysts believe the biopharma sector has significant valuation upside over the next three to five years.
Key Elements
Hengrui Medicine
Fosun Pharma
Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals
Huahai Pharmaceutical
Novartis
Zhang Lianshan
Wang Xingli
Wang Qi
Industrial Securities
FDA
The global biopharmaceutical industry is iterating at a pace that exceeds expectations. While multinational giants like Novartis build patent moats with annual R&D spending in the tens of billions of dollars, Chinese pharmaceutical companies stand at a critical inflection point—facing external pressure from a deeply restructured global competitive landscape, and internal headwinds from domestic homogenization and low-level "involution."
Yet amid the pressure, a clear throughline is emerging: innovative drugs and globalization have become the twin engines driving high-quality growth for Chinese pharma companies. Data shows that in the first half of 2026, China's innovative drug out-licensing (BD) deals totaled approximately $110 billion, already surpassing 80% of the full-year 2025 level and setting a record high for the same period. Deal structures have also upgraded from last year's "single star molecule" model to "platform-based BD."
"Innovative drugs are the only path for the transformation and upgrading of China's pharmaceutical industry. The road is long, but the direction is certain," said Zhang Lianshan, director and vice president of Hengrui Medicine, at a recent industry forum.
From fast-follow to differentiation: R&D investment keeps climbing
Many listed Chinese pharma companies have long made innovative drugs a core transformation priority. Zhang Lianshan explained that Hengrui Medicine has always treated technological innovation as its top development strategy, with cumulative R&D investment now exceeding 50 billion yuan (approximately $7.5 billion), ranking among the highest in China's pharmaceutical industry. The company operates 15 R&D centers across Asia, Europe, the United States, and Australia, with a global R&D team of more than 5,600 people. To date, the company has secured approval for 27 Class 1 innovative drugs and 6 Class 2 new drugs in China, with over 100 proprietary innovative products in clinical development and more than 400 clinical trials underway domestically and internationally—forming a virtuous cycle of "one batch on the market, one batch in clinical trials, one batch in development."
Innovative drugs have become the core growth engine for Fosun Pharma. Data shows that in 2025, Fosun Pharma's innovative drug revenue reached 9.893 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion), with its share of pharmaceutical business revenue rising to 33.16%. The company focuses on three core therapeutic areas—oncology (solid tumors and hematologic malignancies), immunology and inflammation, and neurodegenerative diseases—strengthening its pipeline through independent R&D, collaborative development, and in-licensing.
Huahai Pharmaceutical and Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals likewise place innovative R&D at the center of their strategies. Huahai Pharmaceutical's innovative drug development is guided by a focus on unmet clinical needs and efficient execution, building a future-oriented product pipeline with global competitive advantages. Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals has built end-to-end R&D capabilities spanning from original innovation to industrialization, with its core technologies earning the second prize of the National Science and Technology Progress Award and the China Patent Gold Award, and securing invention patent grants in multiple countries and regions through PCT international applications.
Balancing generics and innovation: cash flow management, not an either-or choice
Generics are the foundation; innovative drugs are the new engine. How to balance the two is the central challenge of pharma transformation.
Wang Qi, CFO and executive vice president of Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals, believes resource allocation is the core issue in pharma transformation. Generics form the bedrock of a company's survival and growth—the primary source of cash flow that sustains innovative R&D. Innovative drugs represent the future growth pole, determining the ceiling of long-term development.
"This is not an either-or choice; it's a cash flow management problem. Internally, we have a broad framework: cash flow generated by generics and mature products covers the R&D spending on innovative drugs," said Zhang Lianshan.
Wang Qi further noted that the key lies in recognizing one's own endowments. Biotechs excel at frontier target exploration and technological breakthroughs, making them suited for first-in-class development; traditional pharma companies excel at industrialization capabilities and market coverage, making them better positioned for differentiated iteration in mature therapeutic areas.
However, Zhu Yonghua, vice president of Huahai Pharmaceutical, sounded a cautionary note. He said the industry's homogenized R&D, low-level duplication, and involution-style competition are constraining the high-quality development of China's pharmaceutical industry. The model of relying solely on generic drug cash flow to fund innovative R&D is no longer sustainable; the innovative drug segment urgently needs to open independent financing channels and cultivate its own cash-generating capacity to ensure efficient advancement of R&D programs.
Hengrui Medicine's view is that involution is essentially a transitional phenomenon in the industry's shift from "imitation" to "innovation"—fast-follow was once a rational, low-risk strategy, but when everyone executes the same strategy, the strategy itself fails. The way out is not retreating to generics, but upgrading: targeting unmet clinical needs, selecting differentiated indications, focusing on controversial or emerging targets, taking on early-stage scientific risk in exchange for exclusivity, and building genuine platform-based technologies.
"We want competition, but rational competition. We hope policy can create a rational competitive environment," said Zhang Lianshan.
Going global enters an efficiency-dividend phase
"Internationalization is an inevitable choice for Chinese pharma companies at this stage of development. The markets that can truly create enormous value are still overseas," said Wang Qi.
Taking the insulin market as an example, the European market structure has been entrenched for over two decades, presenting structural opportunities for latecomers. Hengrui Medicine believes the internationalization opportunity stems primarily from the ongoing patent cliff in U.S. and European markets, an improving policy environment for biosimilar penetration in the United States, and the FDA's strong push in recent years for interchangeability designations.
But going global remains enormously challenging. Wang Qi noted that the bottleneck lies in the EU's extremely stringent review standards—high entry barriers and long review cycles that demand exceptional quality systems and research capabilities. Moreover, after a biosimilar gains approval overseas, there is still a long distance from "market approval" to "market share." Local acceptance of Chinese-made insulin, shifts in physician prescribing habits, and the establishment of commercial channels all represent hard battles requiring long-term investment.
Hengrui Medicine also pointed out that U.S. and European regulated markets demand extremely high standards for manufacturing systems and quality culture, and Chinese companies' GMP systems still face integration costs in aligning with international standards. In the U.S. market, distribution channels are controlled by a handful of large distributors and PBMs, with intense price competition—"the approval is valuable, but selling the product isn't."
In terms of go-global strategy, each company has taken a distinct approach. Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals employs a "three-tier progressive, dynamically balanced" strategy: using its third-generation insulin—which won the vast majority of Class A bids in centralized procurement and holds the industry's second-largest market share—as the cash flow foundation and overseas vanguard; using innovative drugs such as once-weekly/biweekly formulations with significantly reduced injection frequency as the mid-term growth pole; and simultaneously laying out candidates including the fixed-ratio combination weekly formulation GZR102 and the dual insulin analog GZR101 as long-term competitiveness. The three tiers are not an either-or tradeoff, but a progressive relationship of using near-term gains to fund long-term development.
Fosun Pharma's internationalization has been steadily upgrading from "product going global" to "system going global," building a global operating network spanning China, the United States, Europe, Africa, India, and Southeast Asia. In 2025, the company's overseas revenue reached 12.977 billion yuan (approximately $1.9 billion), accounting for 31.15% of total revenue, up 3.64 percentage points year over year.
Currently, Hengrui Medicine has initiated multiple overseas clinical trials for innovative drugs in the United States, Europe, Australia, Japan, and other countries and regions, spanning Phase I through Phase III. The company has obtained approximately 20 overseas marketing authorizations, with products commercialized in more than 50 countries and regions.
AI reshapes the competitive landscape
Under the artificial intelligence trend, AI-driven drug discovery is moving from concept to implementation. Wang Xingli, president of Fosun Pharma, has been deeply involved in AI drug discovery implementation for an extended period. He believes AI technology can cover the entire workflow from drug discovery and molecular screening to clinical trial design optimization, dramatically improving efficiency at every stage.
"AI technology will gradually level the playing field between Chinese pharma companies' engineering talent advantage and the experience advantage of U.S. and European pharma giants. Global leading pharma companies will compete from the same starting line. Under AI's influence, the future core competitiveness of pharma companies will no longer be purchasable public resources like computing power and general-purpose tools, but rather the proprietary knowledge bases and strategic decision-making capabilities that companies accumulate themselves," said Wang Xingli.
Valuation reset: secondary market has yet to fully price in the shift
The pharmaceutical sector in 2026 has shown a clear "first down, then up" pattern—sustained adjustment in the first half, followed by a strong rebound starting mid-June. As of mid-August, the SWS Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index has risen nearly 14% since the start of the second half, significantly outperforming major broad-based indices and becoming one of the market's standout sectors.
However, overall valuations for the biopharma and innovative drug segments remain at relatively low levels. Industrial Securities pharma analysts believe that the valuation of China's innovative drugs must be assessed across two dimensions: the domestic market and overseas markets. Currently, neither the growth potential of the domestic market nor the certain cash flows from going global have been fully reflected in secondary-market valuations.
From the domestic market perspective, analysts note that current secondary-market valuation expectations for innovative drugs remain relatively conservative. China's market potential is enormous, and existing valuation levels are far from reflecting the reasonable value of future product volume growth driving company growth. As innovative drugs continue to penetrate the domestic market and commercialize, the valuation recovery space for domestic operations alone remains vast.
From the going-global perspective, Chinese pharma companies have closed a large number of BD deals over the past few years, but much of the value of these BD deals has not been truly reflected in company valuations. The market has yet to incorporate the certain cash flows from BD partnerships—milestone payments and sales royalties over the next five to ten years—into DCF valuation models, leaving this value significantly underestimated.
"Taken together, over the next three to five years, the biopharma sector has very significant valuation upside, with extremely strong certainty of an upward trajectory amid volatility," said Industrial Securities pharma analysts.
Wang Qi also believes that from an industry fundamentals perspective, China's innovative drug industry faces several structural opportunities: first, population aging continues to expand drug demand; second, medical insurance payment restructuring has reserved greater space for innovative drugs; and third, Chinese pharma companies' R&D efficiency and clinical execution capabilities now hold comparative advantages globally.
Hengrui Medicine noted that in the short term, the pharmaceutical sector may show volatility and divergence, with capital concentrating in companies that have genuine delivery capability, product volume growth, BD deal closures, and positive cash flow, while story-driven names continue to be cleared out. But in the long term, the company remains firmly bullish on the innovative drug industry trend: China's comparative advantage in global R&D efficiency for innovative drugs has been validated; going global has dramatically raised the ceiling on the payment side for innovative drugs; the tipping point for domestic innovative drug approvals and launches has emerged; and leading innovative drug companies will gradually move toward profitability, with the innovative drug sector expected to shift toward earnings-driven investing.
"I believe that within five to ten years, China will definitely produce world-class pharmaceutical companies," said Wang Xingli.

Pharma Industry.content:
The Inauguration and Technology Cooperation Signing Ceremony of the Joint R&D Center for Artificial Intelligence and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Biosynthesis Successfully Held
By:
AB Newswire
August 25, 2026 at 01:12 AM EDT
ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness.
Changsha City, Hunan Province, China - August 25, 2026 -
On the morning of August 16, the inauguration and technology cooperation signing ceremony for the Joint R&D Center for Artificial Intelligence and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Biosynthesis was successfully held at Building 16 of Yuelu Mountain Laboratory.
The center was jointly established by Hunan Yineng Biopharmaceuticals Co., Ltd. (Yineng Pharma), Dongting Laboratory, Hunan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Hunan Agricultural University, and Yuelu Mountain Laboratory.
Academician Yang Shan of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and Director of Dongting Laboratory; Deng Xiaoming, former Director of the China Rural Technology Development Center and a researcher; Yin Wenhui, Deputy Director of the Hunan Provincial Department of Science and Technology; Tong Laisheng, Deputy Mayor of Changsha Municipal People’s Government; Lan Yong, Secretary of the Party Committee of Hunan Agricultural University; Yu Yinghong, President of Hunan Academy of Agricultural Sciences; Yi Yueneng, Chairman of Yineng Pharma; Liu Miao, Party Committee Member and Deputy General Manager of Changsha Investment Holding Group Co., Ltd., representing the shareholder; and Ding Shenghua, Director of the Hunan Institute of Agricultural Product Processing and Quality Safety, along with other leaders and experts, attended the ceremony and participated in the unveiling of the Joint R&D Center.
Cooperation Agreements Signed at the Inauguration Ceremony
During the ceremony, two agreements were signed: the Joint R&D Center Cooperation Agreement and the Achievement Transformation Agreement.
Dr. Yi Yueneng, Chairman of Yineng Pharma, and Ding Shenghua, Director of the Hunan Institute of Agricultural Product Processing and Quality Safety, signed the agreements on behalf of the respective parties.
Witnessed by all the guests present, the center was officially established at the
Hunan Institute of Agricultural Product Processing and Quality Safety
.
Academician Yang Shan: Combining Original Innovation with Industrial Application
Academician Yang Shan expressed his expectations for the newly established Joint R&D Center.
He encouraged all participating parties to value the opportunities provided by the jointly established platform, make full use of Hunan’s resource advantages, and pursue both original innovation and industrial application.
The center should not only deepen basic research but also remain closely focused on actual market needs, producing technological achievements that can be implemented and that possess genuine competitiveness, thereby contributing scientific and technological strength to improving the quality and efficiency of Hunan’s biopharmaceutical industry.
Deng Xiaoming: Focus on AI-Driven Biosynthesis and Core Technologies
In his speech, Deng Xiaoming stated that the R&D center should build on its new starting point and take on its new mission.
The center should take industrial demand as its fundamental direction and technological innovation as its core driver, bringing together scientific research, talent, platform, and industrial resources from the four participating parties.
It will establish regular mechanisms for:
Joint research and development
Resource sharing
Collaborative use of research achievements
The center will focus on key areas including
biosynthesis of pharmaceutical ingredients and AI-driven intelligent drug development
, concentrating resources on overcoming key technological bottlenecks.
The goal is to build an
AI + biosynthesis pharmaceutical ingredient R&D and innovation platform
that is leading in Hunan Province and first-class nationally.
The platform is expected to support the large-scale, high-end, and green development of Hunan’s biopharmaceutical industry, while contributing to the improvement and efficiency enhancement of regional strategic emerging industries.
Hunan Strengthens Collaboration Between Industry, Academia and Research
Yi
n Wenhui, Deputy Director of the Hunan Provincial Department of Science and Technology, emphasized that technological innovation depends on deep integration between industry, academia, and research.
The joint establishment of the R&D center by multiple parties represents a valuable practice for connecting scientific research with industrial development.
According to Yin Wenhui, the participating enterprises, research institutes, universities, and key laboratories should fully leverage their respective strengths, strengthen resource sharing and collaborative research, and accelerate the transformation and implementation of scientific and technological achievements.
Driven by technological innovation, these efforts are expected to further promote
scientific and technological progress and the high-quality development of Hunan’s distinctive biopharmaceutical industry
.
Yineng Pharma: AI + Natural Medicine and Traditional Chinese Medicine Development
Hunan Yineng Biopharmaceuticals Co., Ltd.
is a leading domestic technology empowerment platform for the
AI + natural medicine and full-process development and production of new traditional Chinese medicines
, as well as a leading enterprise in China’s
AI + CRO sector for traditional Chinese medicine
.
As a specialized, sophisticated, and innovative “Little Giant” technology enterprise, Yineng Pharma has established three engineering technology centers covering:
Intelligent research and manufacturing of molecular biopharmaceuticals
Traditional Chinese medicine fingerprinting
Development and industrialization of classical traditional Chinese medicine formulas
The company also has an advanced innovative intelligent traditional Chinese medicine R&D base.
Yineng Pharma has been deeply engaged in the field of
digital and intelligent traditional Chinese medicine
.
By conducting field visits to authentic medicinal material cultivation bases across China and collecting medicinal materials from different harvesting seasons, the company has carried out research involving 2 million batches and accumulated a research dataset containing data at the billion-plus level.
The company has also established
more than 100 classical formula research databases
.
To date, Yineng Pharma has completed preclinical development research for
97 classical formula compound preparations and 29 innovative traditional Chinese medicines
, providing technology empowerment services to
more than 100 organizations across China
.
The establishment of the Joint R&D Center represents an important step in Yineng Pharma’s strategic expansion of its
“AI + biopharmaceuticals”
initiative.
Academician Yang Shan’s Team Advances Biosynthesis Technology
The team led by Academician Yang Shan has long focused on cutting-edge research in synthetic biology.
The team has a cell factory construction laboratory and a pilot-scale biosynthesis validation demonstration line.
It has conducted systematic research into functional natural products such as flavonoids and overcome a number of key technologies related to chassis strain construction and metabolic regulation.
The team has also continued to make progress toward industrialization.
At present, active functional ingredients including naringin, naringenin, and eriodictyol have all reached gram-scale biosynthesis levels, laying a solid foundation for the transition from laboratory research to industrial applications.
The team’s research direction is highly aligned with the biosynthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients, providing strong scientific and technological support for the development of the Joint R&D Center.
AI + Biosynthesis: Connecting Traditional Medicine with Modern Drug Development
The establishment of the Joint R&D Center responds strategically to national initiatives concerning
“AI+” and the “bioeconomy”
.
By deeply integrating advanced AI algorithms with traditional Chinese medicine resources, the center aims to address key industry challenges including the difficulty of obtaining active pharmaceutical ingredients, low production yields, and high costs.
At the strategic level, the initiative is intended to contribute to
Changsha’s development as a global R&D hub city
.
At the industrial level, the center will promote the transformation of traditional Chinese medicine R&D from “experience-based trial and error” to “data-driven” approaches.
Relying on Yineng Pharma’s
AI + CRO platform for digital and intelligent traditional Chinese medicine
, the center will integrate the strengths of research institutes and leading enterprises and connect the entire industrial chain, from natural product discovery to green intelligent manufacturing.
This is intended to provide a model for the digital transformation of traditional Chinese medicine enterprises across China.
Building a Cross-Disciplinary Innovation Platform
At the academic level, the Joint R&D Center will serve as a cross-disciplinary collaborative innovation platform, promoting the integration of fields including:
Artificial intelligence
Biosynthesis
Nutrition and health
Looking ahead, the center will focus on key core technology development and industrial applications.
Through these efforts, the Joint R&D Center aims to make greater contributions to the inheritance and innovation of traditional Chinese medicine and the development of new quality productive forces in the biopharmaceutical industry.
About us
Yineng Pharma is a one-stop, full-process platform for new TCM drug development and production technology enablement. As a national high-tech enterprise specializing in the development of new TCM drugs and natural medicines, Yineng Pharma has grown into a leading TCM CXO company through years of accumulation and development. Its technological capabilities, talent pool, hardware infrastructure, and R&D capacity in digitalized TCM pharmacy are globally leading.

UP & Japan Deepen Healthcare Partnership Across Pharma & Medtech
Hospitals & Govt Health IT
Medical Devices & Diagnostic
Story By
DHN Bureau
•
20 hours ago
•
3 Mins Read
The state also signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with 12 pharmaceutical companies
Uttar Pradesh
and
Japan
have strengthened their healthcare partnership with a focus on pharmaceuticals and medtech.
The collaboration was discussed during the recent visit of Kotaro Nagasaki, Governor of Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, who also met with CM Yogi Adityanath in Uttar Pradesh, focusing on the UP-Japan Healthcare and Care Economy Partnership.
The discussions focused on collaboration across technology adoption, medical education, pharmaceutical development, advanced surgical robotics, medical technology, and skilled healthcare workforce development.
The session brought together government officials, industry representatives, and the Japanese delegation, including Juichi Kobayashi, Director General of the Industrial Policy Department of Yamanashi Prefecture, to discuss opportunities for deeper cooperation in healthcare, medical technology, pharmaceuticals, and workforce development
Sharing thoughts on the partnership, Additional Chief Secretary (Health) Amit Ghosh, said, “The state is advancing robotics-assisted healthcare and specialised medical device manufacturing in collaboration with Japanese partners.”
Elaborating on the state’s medtech initiative, he stated that a 400-acre Medical Tech Park is planned in Uttar Pradesh to support medical innovation and technology development.
Highlighting the investment potential, he added that Japanese companies are showing keen interest in investing in Uttar Pradesh, while efforts are also underway to bring Japanese technology to the state, noting that new possibilities for collaboration in robotics are also being explored.
Beyond medtech, the state also signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with 12 pharmaceutical companies and is engaging Japanese institutional investors for the development of new medical colleges under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model.
The combination of Japan’s work culture and technological expertise with Uttar Pradesh’s expanding healthcare infrastructure is expected to create a strong and sustainable development model, Ghosh stated.
Highlighting the expansion of Uttar Pradesh’s public healthcare infrastructure,
Deputy Chief Minister Brajesh Pathak
noted that the number of operational medical colleges in the state has increased from 47 to more than 83.
The state has also expanded seats across MBBS, MD, nursing, and paramedical programmes.
Further, to address Japan’s growing demand for qualified healthcare professionals, Uttar Pradesh plans to facilitate the deployment of certified doctors, pharmacists, nurses and medical technicians.
The initiative will include specialised language training and orientation on Japanese workplace practices.
The latest initiative is built on Uttar Pradesh's ongoing efforts to expand its healthcare and medtech capabilities through international partnerships.
The development comes after
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath’s recent Japan visit,
during which he met CEOs and senior representatives of Japanese companies and invited them to explore investment opportunities in Uttar Pradesh, including in medical device manufacturing.
A key focus of his discussions was the Medical Device Park being developed in the YEIDA region, which he described as a golden opportunity for Japanese companies.

The Financial Supervisory Service's building is seen in Yeouido, Seoul on June 25, 2026. AJP Ryu Yuna
SEOUL, August 24 (AJP) - The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) will hold four briefings in September to help pharmaceutical and biotech companies adapt to new disclosure rules, the financial watchdog said Monday.
The sessions are intended to help market participants understand the revised requirements before they take effect, reducing the risk of filing errors that could lead to correction requests and delays in fundraising or listing schedules.
The regulator will hold separate meetings for KOSDAQ-listed companies on Sept. 1, underwriters on Sept 8, companies preparing for an initial public offering (IPO) on Sept 15 and KOSPI-listed firms on Sept 21. Each session will focus on the disclosure issues most relevant to that group.
The briefings follow changes announced by the regulator on July 30 to strengthen disclosure requirements for pharmaceutical and biotech companies, particularly those whose value depends heavily on drugs and technologies still under development.
Under the revised rules, companies preparing to go public will have to provide more detail on the assumptions used to determine their IPO prices. These include the expected market size for a drug, its chances of success in clinical trials, the risk of the drug failing to win regulatory approval, and the expected time and cost of development.
The changes are intended to help investors better assess whether an IPO price is reasonable, especially for drug developers that may not yet generate meaningful profits and are valued largely on future earnings expectations.
Disclosure requirements will also be expanded for listed companies. They will have to provide more information on technology licensing agreements, including the size and structure of the deals, as well as the history of transactions involving drugs under development, making it easier for investors to track the candidate's progress.
AJP Takeaways
•  The Financial Supervisory Service will hold four briefings in September 2026 to help pharmaceutical and biotech companies, IPO underwriters and listed firms comply with revised disclosure requirements.
•  The sessions will be held for KOSDAQ-listed companies on Sept. 1, IPO underwriters on Sept. 8, companies preparing to go public on Sept. 15 and KOSPI-listed companies on Sept. 21.
•  Under disclosure changes announced on July 30, 2026, companies preparing for an IPO must provide more detail on how they determine their offering prices, including expected drug market size, clinical-trial success rates, regulatory approval risks, and expected development time and costs.
•  Listed pharmaceutical and biotech companies will also have to disclose more information on technology licensing agreements, including deal size, structure and transaction history involving drugs under development.
Ryu Yuna

Pharma Industry.content:
BT Slingsby Says Japan's Best Drug Assets Have Been Left on the Shelf
Add to Google Preferred Sources
BT Slingsby, founder of Catalys Pacific, has built Japan's largest life-science venture firm around a simple observation: the country produces world-class molecules but fails to turn them into global companies, while its patients simultaneously wait years for Western biotech innovations. In a conversation on BioVenture Voices, Slingsby traced the origins of this dual failure — and the company-creation model he built to fix it. Catalys Pacific runs a two-pronged strategy: spinning Japanese pharmaceutical assets into US-based biotech companies, and building Japanese companies to develop and commercialize Western assets regionally. The track record since 2019 includes roughly a dozen companies created, multiple IPOs and acquisitions, and flagship asset Mineralys reaching a $2.5 billion valuation after going public in early 2023's "nuclear winter." Slingsby's path — from childhood in Egypt, to triathlon world championships, to clinical epidemiology in Kyoto, to the GHIT Fund — supplied the sourcing relationships that became the firm's commercial edge. The open question is whether the model scales beyond its initial strategic anchors, but Slingsby's move back to Tokyo next year signals where he expects the next phase of value creation to occur.
Key Elements
BT Slingsby
Catalys Pacific
Mineralys
Global Health Innovation Technology Fund
Tachi Yamada
Eisai
Takeda
Chugai
Crystalis
Aerialis
Accelus
Travere Therapeutics
Frazier Life Sciences
Chris Garabedian
Haruo Naito
When BT Slingsby was 13 years old, he saw a man in Egypt disabled by elephantiasis — a condition caused by an untreated mosquito bite. That single encounter set him on a path to medicine. Three decades later, the disease that shaped his childhood became the proof-of-concept for a venture model he now runs at scale: taking Japan's deprioritized pharmaceutical assets and building companies around them.
Slingsby, founder and managing director of Catalys Pacific, told BioVenture Voices host Chris Garabedian that Japan's drug development ecosystem has a structural problem. The country produces Nobel-level science and blockbuster small molecules, but systematically fails to convert them into global companies. At the same time, Japanese patients are left waiting for Western biotech innovations that never reach them. "The clinical outcomes because of it actually are better than the United States, because the family is so involved," Slingsby said, describing Japan's family-integrated approach to treating lifestyle diseases. "You have better adherence, you have better compliance, and with that better outcomes." The paradox is that this same sophisticated healthcare system doesn't get first access to some of the most advanced therapies being developed elsewhere.
Catalys Pacific exists to close both gaps. The firm runs a dual inbound/outbound strategy: it spins Japanese pharmaceutical assets out into US-based biotech companies, and it builds Japanese companies to develop and commercialize Western biotech assets regionally. The model has produced roughly a dozen companies since 2019, multiple exits, and a flagship asset that reached a $2.5 billion valuation.
The unconventional path that built the sourcing engine
Slingsby's route to venture capital is deliberately non-linear, and it explains why his firm can do what generalist investors cannot. After pre-med and philosophy at Brown University, he chose not to go straight to medical school. Instead, he earned an MPH and PhD in Japan to study comparative US–Japan clinical outcomes — work that required him to learn Japanese from the ground up, including the local Kyoto dialect, through a Blakemore Fellowship. He failed the Kyoto University entrance exam once before passing on a second attempt. He finished his formal education with an MD from George Washington University at age 33.
A parallel athletic career shaped his approach to drug development. At 12 or 13, a middle-school history teacher — two-time Olympian Bill Leach — introduced him to triathlon. Slingsby made the national team within two years, won world championships in his age group, and struck a deal with his parents: get into a top university, or turn professional. He chose academia, but credits the sport with his resilience:
"It's that work ethic and really trying to focus on the sound and ignore the noise. And, you know, when you're beaten out and there's a lot of failures in this industry... to get back on your horse and charge ahead."
His pivot from clinical academia to industry came through Dr. Haruo Naito, CEO of Eisai, whom he met while teaching clinical epidemiology at Keio University. Naito offered him roles spanning corporate strategy, M&A, and global access — work that introduced him to Tachi Yamada, the late GSK and Gates Foundation leader who became a close mentor and, later, a co-architect of Catalys Pacific's predecessor fund.
GHIT Fund: the $100 million proof-of-concept
Before Catalys Pacific, there was the Global Health Innovation Technology Fund (GHIT). The idea emerged from conversations between Slingsby and Yamada, who were frustrated that Japan's rich pharmaceutical R&D history was not being deployed against global health threats like malaria, tuberculosis, and lymphatic filariasis — the disease Slingsby had encountered in Egypt as a child.
The structure was a public-private matching fund with three layers:
Contributor
Amount
Top Japanese pharmaceutical companies
$25M
Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
$25M
Government of Japan (MHLW + MOFA)
$50M
Total
$100M
The governance was complex — a council of donors, an independent board including Peter Piot, and a selection committee functioning as an investment committee. Slingsby noted that the two Japanese ministries involved had never before collaborated on a joint initiative. The fund was replenished around 2018 to roughly $300–400 million.
GHIT's core thesis — sourcing deprioritized assets from Japanese pharma R&D pipelines and repositioning them for neglected diseases — validated the idea that Japanese innovation was being left on the shelf. It also supplied the "special sauce" for the commercial venture that followed: direct relationships with R&D leadership across Japanese pharma, and an understanding of how each company prioritizes and deprioritizes assets.
The dual model: outbound and inbound
Catalys Pacific launched in 2019 with an investor base anchored by Takeda, followed by Eisai, Chugai, Fujifilm, and later SoftBank. The initial strategic backing of roughly $80–100 million was supplemented by financial institutions once the model demonstrated traction. Slingsby emphasized that Fund I leaned heavily on relationships with established US venture firms — Frazier, Abingworth, and Domain — who co-created companies like Fathom, Hilvax, and Resida.
The firm's structure maps cleanly onto its two strategies:
The outbound companies are not me-too plays. Slingsby framed them as vehicles for advancing science around specific disease etiologies. Mineralys, for example, was built to break open the aldosterone-driven etiology of hypertension. Aerialis, a San Diego-based company, focuses on NMDA-receptor encephalitis as a specific cause of encephalopathy. The drug development itself is the scientific instrument:
"What we're doing there, again, is driving for the science around the etiology of NMDA receptor-driven encephalopathy via drug development to drive that science forward."
Accelus and the economics of Japan-only development
The inbound strategy runs through Accelus, a platform company owned and managed by Catalys Pacific in Japan. Its purpose is to address a growing access gap: as US and European biotechs increasingly commercialize their own drugs rather than licensing to big pharma, they focus on US markets, leaving Japan underserved. Accelus provides the clinical development and commercialization infrastructure to bring those assets to Japanese patients.
The economics differ fundamentally from US drug development, and Slingsby was explicit about why the model is capital-efficient:
"It's very doable in Japan because you're not looking at, you know, you don't need to procure or raise another five or 600 million dollars to commercialize a drug in Japan while you do that in the United States."
The intended end-state for inbound companies is independent commercialization, not immediate sale. The Travere deal illustrates how the model works in practice: Catalys Pacific licensed Japan-Korea rights, built a company around the asset, and ultimately sold to Chugai for roughly $100 million upfront plus near-$100 million in earnouts. But Slingsby stressed that the sale was not the plan — the company was built to develop and commercialize the drug itself, and the Chugai transaction emerged along the way. The same pattern held for Aculous, a narcolepsy/epilepsy asset company that also exited via acquisition.
The track record and the shifting Asian landscape
Mineralys, the firm's flagship, went public in early 2023 — during what Slingsby described as a "nuclear winter" for biotech IPOs — and reached a $2.5 billion valuation. Slingsby has since stepped down as chair, handing the role to an independent director. Crystalis, the company that connected Garabedian and Slingsby, was built around a product already used in Japan, licensed for US and European rights from Fortress Bio — a deal involving an equity position plus downstream royalties.
On the broader Asian landscape, Slingsby sees a structural shift underway. Japan has long produced Nobel-level science, but the region is now generating more first-in-class assets, not just me-toos. He pointed to emerging innovation pockets in Korea and Singapore alongside China's continued maturation.
"We're seeing many more assets coming out of China and not only me-toos, but actually first in class. That's going to continue."
The strategic implication for Catalys Pacific is twofold: Asia is becoming a richer sourcing ground for outbound deals, while the inbound side addresses a genuine access deficit for Japanese patients. The firm is positioned at the intersection of both trends.
The open question is scalability. Catalys Pacific's Fund I leaned heavily on co-creation with established US firms and strategic Japanese anchors. Whether the model can sustain its exit velocity as it moves beyond those initial relationships — and whether the inbound model can consistently reach independent commercialization rather than early acquisition — will determine whether this is a durable asset class or a relationship-driven niche.
Slingsby's own answer to that question is implicit in his next move. He currently splits time between Seattle and Tokyo, but plans to move back to Japan next year. For a physician-scientist who spent his career building bridges between two ecosystems, the signal is clear: the next phase of value creation is in Tokyo. As he reflected on the work itself, there was no hedging about its significance:
"It's great to work in this industry. It's really a privilege. It is absolutely a privilege."

Pharma Industry.content:
DRL, Emcure get approval to make breakthrough HIV drug
IANS
HIV medicine Lenacapavir could soon be available in India
Synopsis
India's drug regulator has cleared the path for local lenacapavir manufacturing. Two Indian pharmaceutical companies received waivers for local clinical trials. This move will improve access to the HIV prevention injection. Lenacapavir is a breakthrough twice-yearly injection for HIV prevention. Patient groups had urged the regulator to expedite this process.
By
Teena Thacker
,
ET Bureau
Aug 25, 2026, 12:32:00 AM IST
Follow us
New Delhi: Lenacapavir, a breakthrough twice-a-year injection used in the prevention of HIV infections, could soon be available in India.
ADVERTISEMENT
India's drug regulator has cleared the path for two Indian pharmaceutical companies to manufacture it, a move that could dramatically improve access to the drug for millions in India and other low- and middle-income countries.
In a meeting held this month, the subject expert committee under the
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(
CDSCO
) recommended local phase III and bioequivalence-trial waivers for
generic lenacapavir
by
Dr Reddy's Laboratories
and
Emcure Pharmaceuticals
. It has, however, asked the companies to conduct a phase IV efficacy study.
Also read:
Indian pharma has little reason to fear Trump
Regulator asks pharma companies to conduct phase-4 efficacy study of ‘lenacapavir’ and submit it to CDSCO
During the meeting, Dr Reddy's presented its proposal for grant of permission for manufacturing and marketing the injection in 463.5 mg/1.5 ml strengths along with justification for phase III clinical trial and bioequivalence-study waivers.
The committee noted that the drug was approved in the US, UK, Canada, the European Union, Australia and a few other countries, according to the minutes of the meeting that ET has seen. The committee reviewed the data presented by Dr Reddy's from the innovator, agreed that pre-exposure prophylaxis, or preventive measures, to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV in adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg who are at increased risk was an unmet medical need in India, and recommended the waivers, the minutes showed.
ADVERTISEMENT
Emcure also presented its proposal and received similar waivers.
The waiver comes with a condition. The companies must conduct a phase IV post-marketing study in India with efficacy as the primary endpoint and must submit the study protocol to CDSCO within three months of receiving marketing authorisation.
ADVERTISEMENT
ADVERTISEMENT
On the question of using lenacapavir for heavily treatment-experienced patients with multidrug-resistant HIV, the committee did not recommend a waiver, citing insufficient evidence on how the drug behaves in the Indian population in terms of pharmacokinetics and ethnicity-related factors.
Also read:
Health Ministry announces medical device regulatory reforms for ease of doing business
ADVERTISEMENT
Patient groups and civil society organisations working on HIV and AIDS across the Asia-Pacific region, including Third World Network, earlier wrote to CDSCO urging it to waive the local trial requirements for generic lenacapavir, arguing that the extensive international evidence already available made duplicating those trials unnecessary and that any delay would only push back access to a drug that people urgently need.
In 2024, half a dozen drug makers including four Indian companies entered into nonexclusive, royalty-free licensing agreements with the drug's developer, Gilead Sciences, to manufacture its generic versions and market it locally and in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
ADVERTISEMENT
While Gilead filed patents widely on the drug, the voluntary licence was meant to overcome the patent barriers for sale in identified low- and middle-income countries.

Pharma Industry.content:
Discussing Regulatory Direction with Local Food, Drug, and Halal Authorities
Phased Approach from Cosmetics and Health Functional Foods to Pharmaceuticals
Targeting GMP Approval for the Cikarang Plant by 2027
Daewoong Pharmaceutical is strengthening its strategy to target the local market by proactively responding to Indonesia's mandatory halal certification, which will be implemented in October 2026.
On August 25, Daewoong Pharmaceutical announced that it is participating in the "Public-Private Joint Support Group for Entry into Indonesia" led by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and attended the "Indonesia Market Entry Companies Meeting" held in Jakarta, Indonesia last month.
On July 21, at the KOTRA Trade Office in Jakarta, Indonesia, participants are discussing local halal regulation response measures during the “Indonesia Market Entry Companies Meeting.” Daewoong Pharmaceutical
View original image
This meeting was organized to support local market entry for domestic pharmaceutical, biotech, and cosmetics companies. Daewoong Pharmaceutical confirmed the direction of local regulations in discussions with representatives from Indonesia's National Agency of Drug and Food Control (BPOM) and Halal Product Assurance Agency (BPJPH), regarding import customs clearance requirements, ingredient safety evaluations, halal labeling, and the schedule for the mandatory certification.
Indonesian authorities shared operating policies for requirements such as the labeling and management of halal and non-halal products. The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and domestic companies also reconfirmed that halal certificates issued by organizations under Korea's mutual recognition agreement (MRA) have the same validity locally after registration in Indonesia. The Ministry proposed to the Indonesian side measures to reduce the onsite inspection burden for certified factories and to extend grace periods for products already in distribution.
Daewoong Pharmaceutical plans to implement phased responses for each product group, ranging from cosmetics and health functional foods to pharmaceuticals. With the mandatory halal certification for ethical pharmaceuticals (ETC) set for October 2034, the company is aiming for GMP approval by July 2027 and is currently constructing the 'Cikarang Solid Dosage Smart Factory.'
The Cikarang plant is being built to accommodate halal certification from the design stage, and Daewoong Pharmaceutical intends to utilize this facility as a production hub for Indonesia and other ASEAN markets.

This week, India's stock market is about to get very busy
Ten companies are lining up to raise over ₹3,500 crore from investors between August 24 and August 31, 2026, one of the busiest IPO weeks India has seen in a while. Six of these are mainboard companies heading straight to the BSE and NSE, while four are smaller SME issues listing on dedicated platforms. From pharma and jewellery to forensic data and hospitals, this week's line-up covers an unusually wide mix of businesses. Here's the full breakdown, company by company.

/
12
Symbiotec Pharmalab: The week's biggest bet
Symbiotec Pharmalab is the heavyweight of the week, aiming to raise ₹1,757 crore, the largest issue on offer. The price band is set between ₹938 and ₹988 per share, with the issue opening on August 24 and closing on August 27, 2026. The pharmaceuticals and biotech company has already locked in ₹526 crore from anchor investors ahead of the public offer, a strong early signal of institutional interest before retail investors even get a look in.

3
/
12
Lumino Industries: Powering India's grid ambitions
Lumino Industries is looking to raise ₹700 crore through its IPO, with a price band of ₹78 to ₹82 per share. The issue opens on August 27 and closes on August 31, 2026, the latest closing window of all six mainboard offers this week. The company operates in power transmission and infrastructure, manufacturing equipment and running EPC contracts for electricity and utility projects, a sector riding India's ongoing push to expand and modernise its power grid.
Agencies
4
/
12
Skyways Air Services: Betting on global logistics
Skyways Air Services is targeting ₹582.80 crore with shares priced between ₹131 and ₹138. The offer opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The company operates in air freight and logistics, and plans to use the funds raised to drive global expansion and build out its infrastructure, a bet on India's growing role as a logistics and trade hub.
Agencies
5
/
12
Annu Projects: Building India, one contract at a time
Annu Projects is raising ₹175.06 crore through a purely fresh issue, priced between ₹94 and ₹99 per share. The IPO opens on August 25 and closes on August 28, 2026. The company works in engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), and since this is a fresh issue rather than an offer for sale, all the money raised will go directly into the company for working capital needs rather than into existing shareholders' pockets.
Agencies
6
/
12
Hy-tech engineers: The precision parts maker
Hy-Tech Engineers is aiming for ₹135.73 crore, with a price band of ₹50 to ₹53 per share. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. Based in Maharashtra, the company manufactures hydraulic fittings and high-precision machinery tools, the kind of unglamorous but essential components that keep India's industrial and manufacturing sectors running.

Priority Jewels: Betting on lightweight luxury
Priority Jewels rounds out the mainboard list, targeting ₹91.50 crore with a price band of ₹190 to ₹200 per share. This is the last mainboard IPO to open this week, launching on August 28 and closing on September 1, 2026. The company is a B2B designer and manufacturer focused on lightweight diamond-studded jewellery, catering to a segment of the luxury market that's grown quickly in recent years.

The SME wave: Smaller companies, bigger risk
Alongside the six mainboard issues, four SME companies are also hitting the market this week, listing on platforms like NSE Emerge and BSE SME rather than the main exchanges. These issues are considerably smaller in size, but come with a catch: SME IPOs typically require a much higher minimum investment from retail investors, often between ₹1 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh per lot, compared to a few thousand rupees for mainboard IPOs.

Madhur Knit Crafts: Weaving in working capital
Madhur Knit Crafts is raising ₹53.28 crore on the NSE SME platform, with shares priced between ₹95 and ₹100. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The Ludhiana-based company manufactures textiles and home products, and plans to use part of the proceeds for green solar capital expenditure alongside general working capital needs.

Sumax Engineering & Kwick Forensic Solutions: Cars and crime-solving
Two more SME issues open mid-week. Sumax Engineering is raising ₹53.40 crore at ₹95 to ₹101 per share, opening August 25 and closing August 28, 2026, focused on the automotive aftermarket with tapes, refinishing and protection components. Kwick Forensic Solutions, listing on BSE SME, is raising ₹50.77 crore at ₹85 to ₹90 per share between August 27 and August 31, 2026 — a fast-growing business supplying forensic data tools and analytics to government and corporate clients.
Agencies
11

ABH Healthcare: A hospital chain goes public
Closing out the SME line-up is ABH Healthcare, raising ₹34.98 crore on the NSE SME platform at a price band of ₹96 to ₹102 per share. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The company runs under the Anil Baghi Hospital brand, operating a 150-bed tertiary care facility in Punjab, a rare healthcare listing in a week otherwise dominated by industrials and consumer names.

Before you apply: Know the risks
With ten IPOs opening in a single week, it's tempting to apply broadly — but not all issues carry the same risk. SME stocks in particular come with lower liquidity, larger lot sizes, and a history of sharp price swings once listed, along with the possibility of capital getting locked up if trading volumes stay thin. Mainboard issues tend to be more stable and liquid, but valuations, business fundamentals and price bands still deserve a close look before you decide where to put your money.

World Health Expo 2027 to spotlight growth in pharma, biotech, longevity
World Health Expo 2027 to spotlight growth in pharma, biotech, longevity
WAM
24th August 2026, 21:00 GMT+11
DUBAI, 24th August, 2026 (WAM) -- World Health Expo (WHX) will expand its focus on pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, longevity and wellness at its 2027 edition, highlighting growth and investment opportunities across some of healthcare's fastest-growing sectors.
Taking place from 25th to 28th January 2027 across Dubai Exhibition Centre, Expo City and Dubai World Trade Centre, WHX will provide a platform for investment, innovation and partnerships shaping these industries.
The expansion comes amid significant healthcare investment across the GCC. According to PwC Middle East, regional healthcare expenditure is projected to reach US$159 billion by 2029, while more than 160 healthcare projects valued at around $53.2 billion are underway.
The global longevity economy is projected to reach $5.4 trillion by 2034, growing by around six to seven percent annually, according to Bank of Singapore. The UAE's longevity market is estimated to reach $32 billion this year, up from $19 billion in 2020, according to the Department of Health - Abu Dhabi.
The global prescription medicine market reached around $1.7 trillion in 2025, increasing ten percent year-on-year, according to IQVIA. Pharmaceutical sales in the Middle East and Africa rose 18 percent, the highest growth among the regions analysed.
Solenne Singer, Senior Vice President - Healthcare at inD, said, "Healthcare investment is expanding rapidly into pharmaceuticals, biotech, longevity and wellness, marking a fundamental shift in where the industry sees future value."
She added that WHX would bring together organisations developing, funding, regulating and implementing next-generation healthcare, connecting these growing sectors with the wider healthcare ecosystem and global investors.
The new Longevity and Wellness sectors will focus on prevention, healthy ageing, precision health and wellness, reflecting the increasing emphasis on preventing disease and extending the number of years people spend in good health.
The Healthspan Stage at Dubai World Trade Centre will host a four-day Longevity and Wellness programme bringing together government leaders, healthcare providers, medical societies and researchers to discuss preventive and metabolic health, the science of ageing, wearable and diagnostic data and evidence-based longevity healthcare.
The new Pharma sector will bring together pharmaceutical companies, biotechnology innovators, manufacturers, researchers, investors and healthcare organisations.
Dubai ranked first globally for greenfield foreign direct investment projects in life sciences in 2025, according to the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, based on Financial Times fDi Markets data. Dubai Science Park is also home to more than 90 laboratories and 6,500 professionals.
Across the GCC, Saudi Arabia's National Biotechnology Strategy aims to establish the Kingdom as the leading biotechnology hub in the Middle East and North Africa by 2030, with biotechnology targeted to contribute more than $34.6 billion to non-oil GDP by 2040.
WHX will also showcase the biotechnology ecosystem through its Biotech and Life Sciences Forum, bringing together pharmaceutical leaders, biotechnology companies, regulators, researchers and investors to examine areas ranging from genomics and precision medicine to clinical trials, biomanufacturing and patient access.
Another addition to WHX 2027 will be the Connections Programme, a week-long networking initiative across two dedicated lounges featuring theme-led group sessions for the healthcare community.
WHX 2027, part of World Healthcare Week alongside WHX Tech and WHX Leaders, is expected to attract more than 90,000 unique attendees and 4,200 exhibitors, with representatives from more than 195 countries.

Daewoong Pharmaceutical(069620)
said on the 25th that it is speeding up halal (products that Muslims can eat and use) certification in Indonesia. Indonesia is the world's fourth-most populous country and is considered an export hub.
In Indonesia, prescription drugs must obtain mandatory halal (products that Muslims can eat and use) certification by Oct. 2034. Daewoong Pharmaceutical is building a Smart Factory in Cikarang, Indonesia, to meet the requirement.
The Smart Factory was designed with halal certification in mind from the establishment stage. The goal is to obtain GMP (good manufacturing practice) approval in July next year and produce solid dosage forms such as capsules and tablets. Daewoong Pharmaceutical said it is pursuing halal certification not only for pharmaceuticals but also for cosmetics and health functional foods.
Daewoong Pharmaceutical is also taking part in the government-private joint task force supporting entry into Indonesia by Korea's government. Lee So-yoon, head of the regulatory and patent center at Daewoong Pharmaceutical, said, "We will raise the profile of K-pharmaceuticals and bio in ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations)."
