Note: Prices are based on a four-week supply; South Korea figures reflect the lowest-priced clinics.
This disparity stems from differences in drug pricing systems. Japan has incorporated Mounjaro into its national health insurance framework as a type 2 diabetes treatment, with the government managing prices. In contrast, South Korea classifies the drug as a non-reimbursed medicine, allowing each medical institution to set its own price. Adding to this, the won-yen exchange rate has fallen to the 800-won level, fueling demand for so-called "sushi-jaero" purchases — buying the drug directly while traveling in Japan.
The problem is that such imports are strictly illegal. While general medications may be brought in for personal use up to six bottles or a three-month supply, Mounjaro and Wegovy are designated as "hazardous pharmaceuticals" by South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, making their importation prohibited regardless of quantity without an import requirement confirmation exemption recommendation. The Korea Customs Service destroys all seized product immediately upon detection at the customs clearance stage.
Nevertheless, tips for evading customs declarations and workaround information — such as claims that "carry-on baggage isn't fully inspected" — circulate openly online. One consumer who reportedly bought a two-month supply in Japan said they avoided detection by hiding the medication in a backpack instead of a handbag. Some local clinics in Japan are even targeting South Korean demand directly, offering Korean-language signage along with KakaoTalk consultation and interpretation services.
Observers note that enforcement alone has clear limitations. Full inspection of all traveler carry-on items is practically impossible, and even when seizures occur, most cases end with confiscation and destruction, as separate penalty provisions remain inadequate. Experts argue that alongside stronger border enforcement, institutional measures are needed to narrow the domestic-overseas drug price gap and reduce the financial burden on patients.

China's innovative drug BD deals top $100 billion in H1; pharma valuation reset window opens
Add to Google Preferred Sources
China's innovative drug industry is at a critical juncture, transitioning from "fast-follow innovation" to "differentiated innovation." In the first half of 2026, China's innovative drug business development (BD) deal value totaled approximately $110 billion, already exceeding 80% of the full-year 2025 level, with deal structures upgrading to "platform-based BD." Companies including Hengrui Medicine, Fosun Pharma, Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals, and Huahai Pharmaceutical continue to ramp up R&D investment while pursuing differentiated global expansion strategies. Meanwhile, AI is reshaping the competitive landscape for global pharma, shifting core competitiveness toward proprietary knowledge bases and strategic decision-making capabilities. Although the SWS Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index has risen nearly 14% since the second half began, secondary-market valuations for innovative drugs remain conservative, with future cash flows from BD deals not yet fully incorporated into DCF models. Industry analysts believe the biopharma sector has significant valuation upside over the next three to five years.
Key Elements
Hengrui Medicine
Fosun Pharma
Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals
Huahai Pharmaceutical
Novartis
Zhang Lianshan
Wang Xingli
Wang Qi
Industrial Securities
FDA
The global biopharmaceutical industry is iterating at a pace that exceeds expectations. While multinational giants like Novartis build patent moats with annual R&D spending in the tens of billions of dollars, Chinese pharmaceutical companies stand at a critical inflection point—facing external pressure from a deeply restructured global competitive landscape, and internal headwinds from domestic homogenization and low-level "involution."
Yet amid the pressure, a clear throughline is emerging: innovative drugs and globalization have become the twin engines driving high-quality growth for Chinese pharma companies. Data shows that in the first half of 2026, China's innovative drug out-licensing (BD) deals totaled approximately $110 billion, already surpassing 80% of the full-year 2025 level and setting a record high for the same period. Deal structures have also upgraded from last year's "single star molecule" model to "platform-based BD."
"Innovative drugs are the only path for the transformation and upgrading of China's pharmaceutical industry. The road is long, but the direction is certain," said Zhang Lianshan, director and vice president of Hengrui Medicine, at a recent industry forum.
From fast-follow to differentiation: R&D investment keeps climbing
Many listed Chinese pharma companies have long made innovative drugs a core transformation priority. Zhang Lianshan explained that Hengrui Medicine has always treated technological innovation as its top development strategy, with cumulative R&D investment now exceeding 50 billion yuan (approximately $7.5 billion), ranking among the highest in China's pharmaceutical industry. The company operates 15 R&D centers across Asia, Europe, the United States, and Australia, with a global R&D team of more than 5,600 people. To date, the company has secured approval for 27 Class 1 innovative drugs and 6 Class 2 new drugs in China, with over 100 proprietary innovative products in clinical development and more than 400 clinical trials underway domestically and internationally—forming a virtuous cycle of "one batch on the market, one batch in clinical trials, one batch in development."
Innovative drugs have become the core growth engine for Fosun Pharma. Data shows that in 2025, Fosun Pharma's innovative drug revenue reached 9.893 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion), with its share of pharmaceutical business revenue rising to 33.16%. The company focuses on three core therapeutic areas—oncology (solid tumors and hematologic malignancies), immunology and inflammation, and neurodegenerative diseases—strengthening its pipeline through independent R&D, collaborative development, and in-licensing.
Huahai Pharmaceutical and Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals likewise place innovative R&D at the center of their strategies. Huahai Pharmaceutical's innovative drug development is guided by a focus on unmet clinical needs and efficient execution, building a future-oriented product pipeline with global competitive advantages. Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals has built end-to-end R&D capabilities spanning from original innovation to industrialization, with its core technologies earning the second prize of the National Science and Technology Progress Award and the China Patent Gold Award, and securing invention patent grants in multiple countries and regions through PCT international applications.
Balancing generics and innovation: cash flow management, not an either-or choice
Generics are the foundation; innovative drugs are the new engine. How to balance the two is the central challenge of pharma transformation.
Wang Qi, CFO and executive vice president of Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals, believes resource allocation is the core issue in pharma transformation. Generics form the bedrock of a company's survival and growth—the primary source of cash flow that sustains innovative R&D. Innovative drugs represent the future growth pole, determining the ceiling of long-term development.
"This is not an either-or choice; it's a cash flow management problem. Internally, we have a broad framework: cash flow generated by generics and mature products covers the R&D spending on innovative drugs," said Zhang Lianshan.
Wang Qi further noted that the key lies in recognizing one's own endowments. Biotechs excel at frontier target exploration and technological breakthroughs, making them suited for first-in-class development; traditional pharma companies excel at industrialization capabilities and market coverage, making them better positioned for differentiated iteration in mature therapeutic areas.
However, Zhu Yonghua, vice president of Huahai Pharmaceutical, sounded a cautionary note. He said the industry's homogenized R&D, low-level duplication, and involution-style competition are constraining the high-quality development of China's pharmaceutical industry. The model of relying solely on generic drug cash flow to fund innovative R&D is no longer sustainable; the innovative drug segment urgently needs to open independent financing channels and cultivate its own cash-generating capacity to ensure efficient advancement of R&D programs.
Hengrui Medicine's view is that involution is essentially a transitional phenomenon in the industry's shift from "imitation" to "innovation"—fast-follow was once a rational, low-risk strategy, but when everyone executes the same strategy, the strategy itself fails. The way out is not retreating to generics, but upgrading: targeting unmet clinical needs, selecting differentiated indications, focusing on controversial or emerging targets, taking on early-stage scientific risk in exchange for exclusivity, and building genuine platform-based technologies.
"We want competition, but rational competition. We hope policy can create a rational competitive environment," said Zhang Lianshan.
Going global enters an efficiency-dividend phase
"Internationalization is an inevitable choice for Chinese pharma companies at this stage of development. The markets that can truly create enormous value are still overseas," said Wang Qi.
Taking the insulin market as an example, the European market structure has been entrenched for over two decades, presenting structural opportunities for latecomers. Hengrui Medicine believes the internationalization opportunity stems primarily from the ongoing patent cliff in U.S. and European markets, an improving policy environment for biosimilar penetration in the United States, and the FDA's strong push in recent years for interchangeability designations.
But going global remains enormously challenging. Wang Qi noted that the bottleneck lies in the EU's extremely stringent review standards—high entry barriers and long review cycles that demand exceptional quality systems and research capabilities. Moreover, after a biosimilar gains approval overseas, there is still a long distance from "market approval" to "market share." Local acceptance of Chinese-made insulin, shifts in physician prescribing habits, and the establishment of commercial channels all represent hard battles requiring long-term investment.
Hengrui Medicine also pointed out that U.S. and European regulated markets demand extremely high standards for manufacturing systems and quality culture, and Chinese companies' GMP systems still face integration costs in aligning with international standards. In the U.S. market, distribution channels are controlled by a handful of large distributors and PBMs, with intense price competition—"the approval is valuable, but selling the product isn't."
In terms of go-global strategy, each company has taken a distinct approach. Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals employs a "three-tier progressive, dynamically balanced" strategy: using its third-generation insulin—which won the vast majority of Class A bids in centralized procurement and holds the industry's second-largest market share—as the cash flow foundation and overseas vanguard; using innovative drugs such as once-weekly/biweekly formulations with significantly reduced injection frequency as the mid-term growth pole; and simultaneously laying out candidates including the fixed-ratio combination weekly formulation GZR102 and the dual insulin analog GZR101 as long-term competitiveness. The three tiers are not an either-or tradeoff, but a progressive relationship of using near-term gains to fund long-term development.
Fosun Pharma's internationalization has been steadily upgrading from "product going global" to "system going global," building a global operating network spanning China, the United States, Europe, Africa, India, and Southeast Asia. In 2025, the company's overseas revenue reached 12.977 billion yuan (approximately $1.9 billion), accounting for 31.15% of total revenue, up 3.64 percentage points year over year.
Currently, Hengrui Medicine has initiated multiple overseas clinical trials for innovative drugs in the United States, Europe, Australia, Japan, and other countries and regions, spanning Phase I through Phase III. The company has obtained approximately 20 overseas marketing authorizations, with products commercialized in more than 50 countries and regions.
AI reshapes the competitive landscape
Under the artificial intelligence trend, AI-driven drug discovery is moving from concept to implementation. Wang Xingli, president of Fosun Pharma, has been deeply involved in AI drug discovery implementation for an extended period. He believes AI technology can cover the entire workflow from drug discovery and molecular screening to clinical trial design optimization, dramatically improving efficiency at every stage.
"AI technology will gradually level the playing field between Chinese pharma companies' engineering talent advantage and the experience advantage of U.S. and European pharma giants. Global leading pharma companies will compete from the same starting line. Under AI's influence, the future core competitiveness of pharma companies will no longer be purchasable public resources like computing power and general-purpose tools, but rather the proprietary knowledge bases and strategic decision-making capabilities that companies accumulate themselves," said Wang Xingli.
Valuation reset: secondary market has yet to fully price in the shift
The pharmaceutical sector in 2026 has shown a clear "first down, then up" pattern—sustained adjustment in the first half, followed by a strong rebound starting mid-June. As of mid-August, the SWS Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index has risen nearly 14% since the start of the second half, significantly outperforming major broad-based indices and becoming one of the market's standout sectors.
However, overall valuations for the biopharma and innovative drug segments remain at relatively low levels. Industrial Securities pharma analysts believe that the valuation of China's innovative drugs must be assessed across two dimensions: the domestic market and overseas markets. Currently, neither the growth potential of the domestic market nor the certain cash flows from going global have been fully reflected in secondary-market valuations.
From the domestic market perspective, analysts note that current secondary-market valuation expectations for innovative drugs remain relatively conservative. China's market potential is enormous, and existing valuation levels are far from reflecting the reasonable value of future product volume growth driving company growth. As innovative drugs continue to penetrate the domestic market and commercialize, the valuation recovery space for domestic operations alone remains vast.
From the going-global perspective, Chinese pharma companies have closed a large number of BD deals over the past few years, but much of the value of these BD deals has not been truly reflected in company valuations. The market has yet to incorporate the certain cash flows from BD partnerships—milestone payments and sales royalties over the next five to ten years—into DCF valuation models, leaving this value significantly underestimated.
"Taken together, over the next three to five years, the biopharma sector has very significant valuation upside, with extremely strong certainty of an upward trajectory amid volatility," said Industrial Securities pharma analysts.
Wang Qi also believes that from an industry fundamentals perspective, China's innovative drug industry faces several structural opportunities: first, population aging continues to expand drug demand; second, medical insurance payment restructuring has reserved greater space for innovative drugs; and third, Chinese pharma companies' R&D efficiency and clinical execution capabilities now hold comparative advantages globally.
Hengrui Medicine noted that in the short term, the pharmaceutical sector may show volatility and divergence, with capital concentrating in companies that have genuine delivery capability, product volume growth, BD deal closures, and positive cash flow, while story-driven names continue to be cleared out. But in the long term, the company remains firmly bullish on the innovative drug industry trend: China's comparative advantage in global R&D efficiency for innovative drugs has been validated; going global has dramatically raised the ceiling on the payment side for innovative drugs; the tipping point for domestic innovative drug approvals and launches has emerged; and leading innovative drug companies will gradually move toward profitability, with the innovative drug sector expected to shift toward earnings-driven investing.
"I believe that within five to ten years, China will definitely produce world-class pharmaceutical companies," said Wang Xingli.

The Emmes Group Names Rama Kondru CEO
Former Veridix CEO to lead Emmes as it expands AI-driven clinical trial innovation.
August 24, 2026
By:
Charlie Sternberg
Associate Editor
, Contract Pharma
♡
Save
Dr. Rama Kondru.
The Emmes Group
has appointed Dr. Rama Kondru as Chief Executive Officer.
Kondru joined the Emmes Group in 2024 and most recently served as CEO of Veridix, the company’s AI, technology, and data sciences business. Kondru has demonstrated leadership in technology-driven innovation across The Emmes Group and brings a combination of scientific expertise, global operating experience, and a track record of scaling technology platforms.
“It is a privilege to lead The Emmes Group at such an exciting time for our industry,” said Kondru. “For nearly five decades, Emmes has stood behind some of the most important public health efforts, from the earliest NIH vaccine and infectious disease programs to the trials that helped the world respond to COVID-19. Building on that legacy, we have a unique opportunity to combine AI, technology, and clinical expertise to transform how trials are designed and conducted. Together with our customers, we will help bring life-changing therapies to patients faster while creating long-term value for customers, employees, and investors.”
Experience
Prior to joining The Emmes Group, Kondru served as Co-CEO of Medidata Solutions, a global leader in cloud-based clinical development technology, where he helped scale one of the industry’s most transformative platforms. He brings 25 years of experience across pharmaceuticals, healthcare technology, data science, and academia, and has built technology-driven businesses that accelerate clinical development and improve patient outcomes.
Earlier in his career, he served as Senior Vice President and Chief Information Officer for Janssen Americas (
Johnson & Johnson
) and Vice President and Chief Information Officer for R&D and Innovation at Johnson & Johnson Medical Devices and held leadership roles at UCB Pharma and F. Hoffmann-La Roche.
Kondru earned his bachelor’s degree from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT Bombay) and his Ph.D. from the University of Pittsburgh, where he also completed postdoctoral research. He has served as an Adjunct Professor at Duke University.

Pharma Associations.content:
– Appointment strengthens board as ANI accelerates transformation into a leading Rare Disease Company –
PRINCETON, N.J., Aug. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- ANI Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (ANI or the Company) (Nasdaq: ANIP) today reported the addition of Henry Gosebruch to its Board of Directors effective August 19, 2026. Mr. Gosebruch brings over 30 years of corporate strategy, business development and finance experience across the biopharmaceutical sector.
“We are excited to add Henry to our Board of Directors during this pivotal moment for the Company,” stated Thomas (Tom) J. Haughey, Chairman of the Board of ANI. “His proven track record in corporate strategy and value-creating acquisitions is expected to strengthen our business development and capital allocation initiatives as we accelerate our transformation to become a leading Rare Disease company. We are delighted to welcome him to the Board, and look forward to his contributions,” he concluded.
“ANI has the management team, the commercial infrastructure and the balance sheet to take a meaningful next step in its evolution via additional business development,” said Mr. Gosebruch. “The Rare Disease franchise is a strong foundation, and I look forward to working with Nikhil, Tom and my fellow directors to help the Company execute the next steps in its transformation.”
Mr. Gosebruch has served as Chief Executive Officer of Lakefront Biotherapeutics NV (formerly Galapagos NV) since May 2025, where he is also a member of the Board of Directors. From July 2023 to February 2025, he served as President and Chief Executive Officer of Neumora Therapeutics, Inc., a publicly traded neuroscience company.
Prior to Neumora, from 2015 to 2023, Mr. Gosebruch was Executive Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer of AbbVie, where he built and led the company’s Corporate Strategy Office, spanning corporate strategy, competitive intelligence, business development and M&A, search and evaluation, alliance management, and AbbVie Ventures. Under his leadership, the group completed more than 100 transactions and investments, including AbbVie’s acquisition of Allergan. Earlier in his career, he spent more than 20 years at J.P. Morgan, most recently as Co-Head of North American M&A.
Mr. Gosebruch serves on the Advisory Board of the University of Pennsylvania Life Sciences & Management Program. He holds a B.S. in Economics from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and is a certified public accountant.
The Company also announced that Muthusamy (Samy) Shanmugam has notified the Board of his decision to resign as a director effective immediately. He will remain in his executive management role as ANI’s Head of Research and Development and Chief Operating Officer of New Jersey Operations.
Mr. Haughey continued, “I want to thank Samy for his dedicated Board service and valuable contributions over the past five years. We will continue to benefit from his insights and deep experience as a member of our executive leadership team.”
About ANI Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
ANI Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: ANIP) is a diversified biopharmaceutical company committed to its mission of “Serving Patients, Improving Lives” by developing, manufacturing, and commercializing innovative and high-quality therapeutics. The Company is focused on delivering sustainable growth through its Rare Disease business, which markets novel products in the areas of ophthalmology, rheumatology, nephrology, neurology, and pulmonology; its Generics business, which leverages R&D expertise, operational excellence, and U.S.-based manufacturing; and its Brands business. For more information, visit https://www.anipharmaceuticals.com.
Forward-Looking Statements
To the extent any statements made in this release deal with information that is not historical, these are forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Such statements include, but are not limited to, statements regarding the Company’s strategy; its expectations regarding its future operations, financial position or revenues, including its 2026 financial guidance; its expectations regarding its share repurchase program; the results and timing of the Company’s preclinical studies, clinical trials, regulatory submissions and regulatory approvals; the commercialization and anticipated sales of the Company’s products, including current and planned product launches and any additional product launches from the Company’s generic pipeline; the Company’s estimates of the market opportunity and addressable patient populations for its products; the expansion and execution capabilities of the Company’s sales force for acute gouty arthritis for Cortrophin Gel; the Company’s anticipated growth opportunities, including for Cortrophin Gel and ILUVIEN; the Company’s positioning for continued shareholder value creation; anticipated R&D developments and clinical trial advances; and other statements that are not historical in nature, particularly those that utilize terminology such as “anticipates,” “will,” “expects,” “plans,” “potential,” “future,” “believes,” “intends,” “continue,” the negatives thereof, or other words of similar meaning, derivations of such words and the use of future dates.
Uncertainties and risks may cause the Company’s actual results to be materially different than those expressed in or implied by such forward-looking statements. Uncertainties and risks include, but are not limited to: the ability of the Company’s approved products, including Cortrophin Gel and ILUVIEN, to achieve commercialization at levels of market acceptance that will allow the Company to maintain profitability; the Company’s ability to complete or achieve any or all of the intended benefits of acquisitions and investments, in a timely manner or at all; delays and disruptions in the production of the Company’s approved products; increased costs and potential loss of revenues if the Company needs to change suppliers due to the limited number of suppliers for its raw materials, active pharmaceutical ingredients, excipients, and other materials; delays and disruptions in the production of the Company’s approved products as a result of its reliance on single source third party contract manufacturing supply for certain of its key products, including Cortrophin Gel and ILUVIEN; delays or failure to obtain or maintain approvals by the FDA of the Company’s products; changes in policy or actions that may be taken by the FDA, United States Drug Enforcement Administration and other regulatory agencies; risks that the Company may face with respect to importing raw materials and delays in delivery of raw materials and other ingredients and supplies necessary for the manufacture of the Company’s products from both domestic and overseas sources due to supply chain disruptions or for any other reason, including increased costs due to tariffs or macroeconomic disruptions; the ability of the Company’s manufacturing partners to meet its product demands and timelines; the impact of changes or fluctuations in exchange rates; the Company’s ability to develop, license or acquire, and commercialize new products; the Company’s obligations in agreements under which it licenses, develops or commercializes rights to products or technology from third parties and its ability to maintain such licenses; the level of competition the Company faces and the legal, regulatory and/or legislative strategies employed by its competitors to prevent or delay competition from generic alternatives to branded products; the Company’s ability to protect its intellectual property rights; the impact of legislative or regulatory reform on the pricing for pharmaceutical products; the impact of any litigation to which the Company is, or may become, a party; the Company’s ability, and that of its suppliers, development partners, and manufacturing partners, to comply with laws, regulations and standards that govern or affect the pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries; the Company’s ability to maintain the services of its key executives and other personnel; and general business and economic conditions, such as inflationary pressures, geopolitical conditions.
More detailed information on these and additional factors that could affect the Company’s actual results are described in the Company’s filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), including its most recent annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, and other periodic reports, as well as other filings with the SEC. Sun Pharmaceutical Industries
has secured a significant legal victory in the United States, with the Third Circuit Court of Appeals affirming summary judgment in its favor regarding antitrust litigation over generic Lipitor (Atorvastatin). The appellate court's decision denies class certification for plaintiffs and brings the long-standing dispute substantially to a close.
The litigation centered on a 2008 patent settlement agreement between Sun Pharma and Pfizer. Plaintiffs alleged that this settlement unlawfully delayed the entry of generic competition for Lipitor into the US market, arguing that absent the agreement, the generic version would have launched earlier.
Legal outcome
The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld the order from the United States District Court. The lower court had previously granted summary judgment in its entirety to Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited and certain of its subsidiaries.

Summary judgment upheld in favor of Sun Pharma and subsidiaries

Denied for plaintiffs

This outcome represents a favorable development for the company, removing a material legal overhang associated with the case. The matter is now considered substantially closed, subject only to any further remedies available to plaintiffs under applicable law.
Regulatory disclosure
The company disclosed the update under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. Sun Pharma has consistently disclosed the status of this matter in its financial statements throughout the duration of the litigation.

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: €2m boost for Ghana pharmaceutical research and vaccine innovation - MyJoyOnline
Pharma Associations.content:
Audio By Carbonatix
Ghanaian research institutions and pharmaceutical companies have secured
€2 million in grants
to develop vaccines, medicines, and other health products for local and regional markets.
Eight projects have been selected under the PharmaVax Ghana programme, which seeks to strengthen collaboration between researchers and pharmaceutical manufacturers and move promising health innovations from laboratories into commercial production.
The grants were announced at a “Research Meets Manufacturing” ceremony held in Accra on August 19.
The initiative is jointly funded by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development and the European Union and implemented by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), in collaboration with Ghana’s National Vaccine Institute.
The selected projects cover a range of health challenges, including malaria, chronic diseases, vaccines, and infectious diseases.
One project will develop a fast-dissolving malaria tablet for children, with the aim of making treatment easier to administer while improving dosing accuracy.
Another project will apply artificial intelligence to support the development of monoclonal antibodies and diagnostics for malaria and Mpox.
Other research teams will investigate locally developed herbal treatments for conditions including hypertension, prostate health, and alcohol-related liver disease.
The projects will also focus on improving the stability and regulatory approval of locally produced vaccines and snake venom antiserum.
The eight projects will receive a combined €2 million in grant funding, with Ghanaian partners contributing an additional €425,000.
Organisers say the programme is designed to address a longstanding challenge of turning scientific research into products that can be manufactured and made available to the public.
The projects were selected from 43 proposals by an independent committee of nine Ghanaian experts.
Selection criteria included technical merit, potential public benefit, participation of a local manufacturer, and the sustainability of the research beyond the grant period.
Beyond the funding, successful teams will receive technical assistance, networking opportunities, and opportunities for knowledge exchange.
Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh said the programme provides an opportunity to bring researchers, manufacturers, government and international partners together to translate scientific discoveries into medicines and vaccines.
Chief Executive of the National Vaccine Institute, Dr Sodzi Sodzi-Tettey, said Ghana has the scientific expertise and an increasingly capable pharmaceutical industry needed to develop health products tailored to local needs.
The investment comes as Ghana seeks to expand its domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and reduce vulnerabilities in the supply of essential medicines and other health products.
The National Vaccine Institute, established in 2023, has been tasked with coordinating Ghana’s efforts in vaccine and sera research, development and manufacturing.
Through PharmaVax Ghana, GIZ is supporting research and development, skills development, regulatory strengthening, technology transfer and investment promotion within the pharmaceutical sector.
German Ambassador to Ghana, Frederik Landshöft, said the partnership would help connect Ghanaian research, manufacturing and innovation with German technology and investment.
He said the objective is to support the local production of medicines and vaccines for Ghana and potentially the wider West African market.
The programme is therefore expected to contribute to a stronger domestic pharmaceutical industry while creating opportunities for Ghanaian innovations to move beyond research institutions into commercial production and regional markets.

Pharma Associations.evidence: 출처:Chosunbiz+28 | 최신:Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:01:00 GMT+5 | 키워드+5 | 순위:176위+2
Pharma Associations.url_match_title: Dong Kook Lifescience partners with Inventera and triples capacity to lead Korea - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
Pharma Associations.content:
Dongkook Pharmaceutical(086450)
group is expanding its contrast agent business and speeding up its move to monopolize the domestic contrast agent market. It plans to move beyond a business centered on generic contrast agents, strengthen partnerships with new drug developers, and expand production capacity, while broadening into contract manufacturing (CMO) to leap forward as a "comprehensive platform" for contrast agents.
On the 25th, according to the pharmaceutical and biotech industry, Dongkook Pharmaceutical subsidiary
Dong Kook Lifescience(303810)
is working to strengthen its market dominance by securing new contrast agent drugs through open innovation and expanding its production and sales base.
(From left) Park Jae-won, CEO of Dong Kook Lifescience, and Shin Tae-hyun, CEO of Inventera. /Courtesy of Dong Kook Lifescience
◇ Domestic No. 1 Dongkook forms a "contrast agent alliance" with strategic investor Inventera
Contrast agents are pharmaceuticals that help interpretation by making organs, blood vessels and tissues appear more clearly in imaging tests such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT).
The domestic contrast agent market is considered a saturated market with strong price-cutting pressure as numerous generic products compete. In the global market, Germany's Bayer leads, while in Korea, Dong Kook Lifescience, Taejoon Pharmaceutical and
Daewoong Pharmaceutical(069620)
compete.
Dong Kook Lifescience focuses on MRI and CT contrast agents and holds the No. 1 market share in the domestic contrast agent market. Market share steadily rose from 16.8% in 2021 to 20.3% in 2022, 21.4% in 2023 and 22.6% in 2024. The contrast agent business accounts for 67.6% of total sales.
Its main products, the nation's first generic X-ray contrast agent "Pami-Ray" and the MRI contrast agent "Uni-Ray," have been approved in 25 countries including Japan and Europe. It has 43 finished goods and five active ingredients, and has built a system that covers the entire contrast agent business, from active ingredient synthesis to finished product manufacturing and sales and distribution.
The area the company has particularly focused on recently is new contrast agent drugs. A key partner is
Inventera(0007J0)
, in which Dongkook Pharmaceutical Group participated as a strategic investor in 2024. Dongkook Pharmaceutical and Dong Kook Lifescience each invested 1.5 billion won, for a total of 3 billion won, thereby securing about 3.6% equity in Inventera for the group.
Inventera developed the nano drug-delivery platform "Invinity" to improve the limitations of iron-based MRI contrast agents by encapsulating the iron component with polysaccharides (polymer carbohydrates). The method wraps the iron component like a protective shield so it acts more safely and stably in the body.
Inventera is developing the MRI contrast agent "INV-002 (NEMO-103)" using this technology. It is the world's first product dedicated to MR arthrography (MRA), which uses MRI to image the inside of joints. The company recently completed phase 3 trials and plans to apply for product approval with the Ministery of Food and Drug Safety within the year.
Currently, there are no MRA-dedicated approved products in Korea, so gadolinium-based intravenous contrast agents are diluted and injected into the joint cavity. This method carries an infection risk during dilution and has the limitation that the contrast agent can quickly leak out of the joint cavity, degrading image quality.
Inventera plans to first apply for approval targeting the shoulder joint, then expand the indication to the elbow, wrist and hip joints. The domestic market size is about 120 billion won, and the global market is projected to reach 8.6 trillion won by 2030.
In 2024, Dong Kook Lifescience also secured the production and distribution rights for NEMO-103, along with exclusive global sales rights in Japan, China and Southeast Asia. Inventera secures a stable production and sales base, while Dong Kook Lifescience adds a new drug to its contrast agent business, which had been centered on generics, creating a growth engine.
Dong Kook Lifescience Anseong Plant
◇ Expanding production capacity through plant expansion… Beyond new drugs to CMO business
Dong Kook Lifescience is increasing production capacity in line with the expansion of its new drug business. At the same time, it plans to use the increased production headroom to expand into contract manufacturing (CMO), leveraging its production base as a new growth engine.
Its production base is the Anseong plant. It has built a system capable of carrying out the entire process in-house, from active ingredient synthesis to finished product manufacturing. The finished drug plant was acquired from Germany's Bayer in 2019, completed Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification in 2021, and went into full operation in the second half of 2022. The active pharmaceutical ingredient plant was newly established in 2021 and has been operating since 2023.
Dong Kook Lifescience is investing 17 billion won in this plant to expand the production building. With this, it plans to boost finished drug production capacity from 2.19 million vials in 2024 to about three times that level by 2028. Active pharmaceutical ingredient production capacity will also increase 23.1% over the same period, from 268 tons (t) to 330 t. The expansion work is scheduled for completion and equipment installation in 2026, GMP approval in 2027, and the start of production in the first half of 2028.
The increased production headroom will also be used to expand the CMO business. Dong Kook Lifescience signed a five-year contract from 2026 to 2031 with a domestic pharmaceutical company for nonionic iodinated contrast agent injections, and a 10-year contract from 2026 to 2036 with another company for an antiplatelet active ingredient.
It is also expanding overseas operations. It has built an export network in 34 countries and exports contrast agents to Europe, Japan, Asia and South America. It also plans to speed up the global market entry of NEMO-103 by leveraging its existing overseas sales network.
It is also pushing into the Chinese market. Late last year, it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) in the contrast agent field with China's Tianyu Pharmaceutical and is discussing the signing of definitive agreements in seven areas, including joint development of an MRI contrast agent new drug, joint development of active pharmaceutical ingredients and export of finished drugs.
Dong Kook Lifescience previously said in IR materials, "We will improve product revenue in the contrast agent business and expand our portfolio, while strengthening new drug development and open innovation, and enhancing global exports and production capacity to increase market competitiveness."

Mainland Chinese technology and pharmaceutical companies are using Hong Kong as a launching pad for global expansion, industry leaders have said, as a major state-owned drugmaker weighs whether to invest in the city’s
Northern Metropolis
megaproject.
The comments highlighting the city’s international background and professional expertise were made during a six-day trip to the rest of the
Greater Bay Area
, which was arranged by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office and started on Sunday.
“Hong Kong is stepping up efforts to develop its innovation and technology sector. Its unique blend of Chinese and Western cultures, along with its high degree of internationalisation, gives the city a clear advantage in developing the traditional Chinese medicine industry,” Chen Jiehui, vice-chairman of Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings, said on Monday.
“Through Hong Kong’s international platform, global languages and standards can be leveraged to help traditional Chinese medicine go global … such as Southeast Asian countries which could serve as a prime example of markets expanding internationally via Hong Kong.”
Chen Jiehui, vice-chairman of Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Holdings, has said his company is considering investing in the Northern Metropolis. Photo: Vivian Au
Chen added that his company, a major state-owned pharmaceutical enterprise, was considering investing in the Northern Metropolis and had previously held alignment discussions with relevant parties. He did not reveal details of the possible investment.
The Northern Metropolis megaproject aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the border with the mainland into a technological and economic hub.

Godrej Industries Group
on Monday said it has signed a
Memorandum of Understanding
(MoU) with the Government of Haryana, outlining a future investment plan of approximately
₹20
,000 crore in the state.
The proposed investment will build on the Group’s existing footprint in Haryana, where it has invested approximately ₹12,000 crore to date and employs around 9,000 people across its businesses, the company said.
Godrej Properties Ltd
(GPL) will be a key driver of the Group’s investment plans. Having invested approximately ₹11,000 crore in Haryana to date, GPL plans to invest a further ₹16,000 crore by FY28, taking its total investment in the state to around ₹27,000 crore.
Advt
According to the company’s statement, GPL currently has 18 projects across Gurugram, Sonipat, Faridabad, Panipat and Kurukshetra, with its future projects expected to create more than 11,000 jobs.
The MoU was signed in the presence of Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini and has the potential to create around 40,000 jobs.
Apart from residential development, Godrej Ventures, the Group’s real estate private equity business, has invested around ₹1,000 crore in Haryana and plans to invest a further ₹3,500 crore in Grade A+ office infrastructure in Gurugram.
Its proposed investments are expected to generate more than 30,000 direct and indirect jobs, further strengthening Gurugram’s commercial ecosystem and its attractiveness to multinational companies and global capability centres (GCCs), the Group said.
“We’re pleased to formalise this next phase of investment through our MoU with the Government of Haryana and look forward to working closely with the state to bring these plans to life,” said Pirojsha Godrej, Chairperson, Godrej Industries Group.
Godrej Capital operates five branches in Haryana and has facilitated approximately ₹550 crore in bookings through its financing business. Godrej Consumer Products has a network of 42 direct distributors and more than 250 rural stockists across the state, the Group said.
The Group also spends approximately ₹1 crore annually on CSR initiatives and more than ₹10 crore on infrastructure-level initiatives in Haryana.

has signed a

The MoU was signed in the presence of Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini.
Godrej Industries Group has invested approximately Rs 12,000 crore in Haryana to date and employs around 9,000 people across its businesses in the state, the company said in a media release on Monday.

Godrej Properties Ltd
(GPL) will be a key driver of the group's investment plans. The company currently has 18 projects across Gurugram, Sonipat, Faridabad, Panipat and Kurukshetra, with its future projects expected to create more than 11,000 jobs.

Godrej Ventures, the group's real estate private equity business, has invested around Rs 1,000 crore in Haryana and plans to invest a further Rs 3,500 crore in Grade A+ office infrastructure in Gurugram. These investments are expected to generate more than 30,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Pirojsha Godrej, Chairperson, Godrej Industries Group, said, "Haryana has emerged as an important growth driver for the Godrej Industries Group. The depth of its economy, the pace of urbanisation and the emergence of Gurugram as a major commercial and employment hub create opportunities across several of our businesses."
He added, "We're pleased to formalise this next phase of investment through our MoU with the Government of Haryana and look forward to working closely with the state to bring these plans to life."
Rakesh Swami, Group Head and President – Corporate Affairs, Godrej Industries Group, said, "We appreciate the ease of doing business and the favourable investment environment the state government has fostered. This MoU reaffirms our confidence in Haryana as a long-term investment destination, with opportunities spanning residential and commercial development to the wider infrastructure and services ecosystem."
The group's other businesses also have an established presence in Haryana. Godrej Capital operates five branches in the state and has facilitated approximately Rs 550 crore in bookings through its financing business.
Godrej Consumer Products
has a network of 42 direct distributors and more than 250 rural stockists across the state.

Godrej Industries Group has also contributed to community and infrastructure initiatives in Haryana, spending approximately Rs 1 crore annually on CSR initiatives and more than Rs 10 crore on infrastructure-level initiatives in the state. Its work includes strengthening support systems for construction workers, providing weather-related insurance, and supporting the restoration and beautification of public spaces in Karnal and Kurukshetra.
The group said it will continue to work with the Government of Haryana to support the state's development priorities and enable further investments across its businesses.
Godrej Industries Group posted revenues of $7.2 billion in FY26 and had a market capitalisation of $19 billion as of March 31, 2026. It operates across FMCG, real estate, financial services, agriculture and chemicals.

Godrej Industries group signs pact to invest Rs 200 billion in Haryana
Godrej Industries group on Monday said ​it has signed ​a pact with the government of Haryana ​to invest 200 billion rupees ($2.09 billion) in the northern state, expanding its presence in the region.
The group has signed a ‌memorandum of ⁠understanding ⁠with the state government with the investment expected to create ​around 40,000 jobs.
Godrej Industries Group, which operates across consumer goods, ​real estate and financial services, has invested about 120 billion rupees in Haryana so far and employs ​around 9,000 people in the ⁠state. The ‌group posted revenue of $7.2 billion in ​fiscal 2026.
Advt
Godrej ​Properties, the group's real estate arm, ⁠will be a key driver of the ​investment and plans to deploy a further ​160 billion rupees in Haryana by fiscal 2028, taking its total investment in the state to around 270 billion rupees.
Godrej Ventures, the group's real estate private equity business, plans to invest another ‌35 billion rupees in office infrastructure in Gurugram. The proposed investment is expected to ​generate more ​than 30,000 ⁠direct and indirect jobs, it said.
"Haryana has emerged as an important growth driver for the Godrej Industries Group," Chairperson ​Pirojsha Godrej said, adding that the group sees the region as a market where it can continue to invest for the long term.
($1 = 95.7250 Indian rupees)
(Reporting by Nishit Navin in Bengaluru; Editing by Sonia Cheema and Nivedita Bhattacharjee)

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: Arcturis and Akrivia agree £140m merger to create major NHS data group - Building Better Healthcare
Pharma Associations.content:
Arcturis Data and Akrivia Health have agreed a £140m all-share merger that will create one of the UK’s largest healthcare data groups, according to new reporting from Sky News.
The deal is expected to be completed in autumn 2026.
The Oxford-based companies provide NHS patient data and analytics to the pharmaceutical industry, with the combined business expected to have 40 NHS trusts as customers.
The deal, which is expected to complete in autumn 2026, will bring together data covering more than 20 million patients currently receiving treatment and 100 million aggregated patient records.
The combined group is expected to have particular strengths in oncology, neurology and mental health, immunology, and cardiovascular health.
Arcturis and Akrivia already have partnerships with pharmaceutical companies including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, GSK, Johnson & Johnson, Novartis and Teva.
The merger comes amid continuing debate over the use of patient and healthcare data in the NHS, including the role of US technology company Palantir.
Palantir is developing the Federated Data Platform for NHS England, with recent forecasts suggesting the expected cost of the platform could rise to as much as £1.1bn.
The proposed merger would create a UK-owned and UK-domiciled healthcare data company, according to industry sources.
What does each data company do?
Arcturis, formerly known as Sensyne Health, was rescued in 2022 following financial difficulties through a £26m recapitalisation.
The company subsequently raised a further £10m from investors including Lansdowne Partners and Salica Investments.
Akrivia Health was founded in 2019 as a spinout from the University of Oxford and the NHS.
It was built around the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system.
The management structure of the combined business has not yet been confirmed.
Akrivia chief executive David Newton is expected to take a senior position in the new company, while Arcturis chief executive Alex Snow is also expected to remain in a leadership role.
The proposed transaction is subject to completion in the autumn.

10 IPOs, ₹3,500 crore this week: From pharma to forensics, all names, dates & prices
Curated by
Lavanya Mallidi
, ET Online
|
Aug 25, 2026, 09:30:04 AM IST
1
/
12
This week, India's stock market is about to get very busy
Ten companies are lining up to raise over ₹3,500 crore from investors between August 24 and August 31, 2026, one of the busiest IPO weeks India has seen in a while. Six of these are mainboard companies heading straight to the BSE and NSE, while four are smaller SME issues listing on dedicated platforms. From pharma and jewellery to forensic data and hospitals, this week's line-up covers an unusually wide mix of businesses. Here's the full breakdown, company by company.
ET Online
2
/
12
Symbiotec Pharmalab: The week's biggest bet
Symbiotec Pharmalab is the heavyweight of the week, aiming to raise ₹1,757 crore, the largest issue on offer. The price band is set between ₹938 and ₹988 per share, with the issue opening on August 24 and closing on August 27, 2026. The pharmaceuticals and biotech company has already locked in ₹526 crore from anchor investors ahead of the public offer, a strong early signal of institutional interest before retail investors even get a look in.
Agencies
3
/
12
Lumino Industries: Powering India's grid ambitions
Lumino Industries is looking to raise ₹700 crore through its IPO, with a price band of ₹78 to ₹82 per share. The issue opens on August 27 and closes on August 31, 2026, the latest closing window of all six mainboard offers this week. The company operates in power transmission and infrastructure, manufacturing equipment and running EPC contracts for electricity and utility projects, a sector riding India's ongoing push to expand and modernise its power grid.
Agencies
4
/
12
Skyways Air Services: Betting on global logistics
Skyways Air Services is targeting ₹582.80 crore with shares priced between ₹131 and ₹138. The offer opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The company operates in air freight and logistics, and plans to use the funds raised to drive global expansion and build out its infrastructure, a bet on India's growing role as a logistics and trade hub.
Agencies
5
/
12
Annu Projects: Building India, one contract at a time
Annu Projects is raising ₹175.06 crore through a purely fresh issue, priced between ₹94 and ₹99 per share. The IPO opens on August 25 and closes on August 28, 2026. The company works in engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), and since this is a fresh issue rather than an offer for sale, all the money raised will go directly into the company for working capital needs rather than into existing shareholders' pockets.
Agencies
6
/
12
Hy-tech engineers: The precision parts maker
Hy-Tech Engineers is aiming for ₹135.73 crore, with a price band of ₹50 to ₹53 per share. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. Based in Maharashtra, the company manufactures hydraulic fittings and high-precision machinery tools, the kind of unglamorous but essential components that keep India's industrial and manufacturing sectors running.
Agencies
7
/
12
Priority Jewels: Betting on lightweight luxury
Priority Jewels rounds out the mainboard list, targeting ₹91.50 crore with a price band of ₹190 to ₹200 per share. This is the last mainboard IPO to open this week, launching on August 28 and closing on September 1, 2026. The company is a B2B designer and manufacturer focused on lightweight diamond-studded jewellery, catering to a segment of the luxury market that's grown quickly in recent years.
Agencies
8
/
12
The SME wave: Smaller companies, bigger risk
Alongside the six mainboard issues, four SME companies are also hitting the market this week, listing on platforms like NSE Emerge and BSE SME rather than the main exchanges. These issues are considerably smaller in size, but come with a catch: SME IPOs typically require a much higher minimum investment from retail investors, often between ₹1 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh per lot, compared to a few thousand rupees for mainboard IPOs.
Agencies
9
/
12
Madhur Knit Crafts: Weaving in working capital
Madhur Knit Crafts is raising ₹53.28 crore on the NSE SME platform, with shares priced between ₹95 and ₹100. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The Ludhiana-based company manufactures textiles and home products, and plans to use part of the proceeds for green solar capital expenditure alongside general working capital needs.
Agencies
10
/
12
Sumax Engineering & Kwick Forensic Solutions: Cars and crime-solving
Two more SME issues open mid-week. Sumax Engineering is raising ₹53.40 crore at ₹95 to ₹101 per share, opening August 25 and closing August 28, 2026, focused on the automotive aftermarket with tapes, refinishing and protection components. Kwick Forensic Solutions, listing on BSE SME, is raising ₹50.77 crore at ₹85 to ₹90 per share between August 27 and August 31, 2026 — a fast-growing business supplying forensic data tools and analytics to government and corporate clients.
Agencies
11
/
12
ABH Healthcare: A hospital chain goes public
Closing out the SME line-up is ABH Healthcare, raising ₹34.98 crore on the NSE SME platform at a price band of ₹96 to ₹102 per share. The issue opens on August 24 and closes on August 27, 2026. The company runs under the Anil Baghi Hospital brand, operating a 150-bed tertiary care facility in Punjab, a rare healthcare listing in a week otherwise dominated by industrials and consumer names.
Agencies
12
/
12
Before you apply: Know the risks
With ten IPOs opening in a single week, it's tempting to apply broadly — but not all issues carry the same risk. SME stocks in particular come with lower liquidity, larger lot sizes, and a history of sharp price swings once listed, along with the possibility of capital getting locked up if trading volumes stay thin. Mainboard issues tend to be more stable and liquid, but valuations, business fundamentals and price bands still deserve a close look before you decide where to put your money.

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: Symbiotec IPO: Tracing How India's API Sector Evolved And Where This Pharma Manufacturer Fits Into That Journey - chandigarhmetro.com
Pharma Associations.content:
Few industries in India have transformed as dramatically over the past three decades as pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing, moving from a period of heavy import dependence to becoming one of the world’s most relied-upon sources for affordable, quality-compliant drug ingredients. This transformation didn’t happen overnight, and tracing its trajectory offers a genuinely different way to understand where a company entering public markets today actually stands. The
Symbiotec IPO
arrives at a moment shaped by decades of industry evolution, and looking at that broader arc reveals more about the business than financial ratios alone ever could.
From Import Dependence To Global Supplier Status
Three decades ago, India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing sector looked dramatically different from what exists today. Much of the country’s drug production relied on imported raw materials and ingredients, with domestic manufacturing capability still developing across most therapeutic categories. Policy reforms around patent law, coupled with sustained private investment in manufacturing infrastructure, gradually shifted this dynamic, allowing Indian companies to build the technical expertise needed to manufacture ingredients that had previously been sourced from abroad.
By the early 2000s, this shift had accelerated considerably, with Indian API manufacturers beginning to secure regulatory approvals from international bodies, opening doors to export markets that had previously been largely inaccessible to domestic producers.
What Changed Along The Way
Several developments contributed meaningfully to this transformation over the years:
Investment in quality infrastructure
, allowing facilities to meet increasingly stringent international manufacturing standards
Growing technical talent pool
, developed through India’s expanding pharmaceutical and chemical engineering education base
Policy support for export-oriented manufacturing
, encouraging companies to pursue international certifications
Cost advantages
, which made Indian-manufactured ingredients attractive to global formulators without compromising quality
Each of these factors compounded over time, gradually establishing India as a manufacturing base that global pharmaceutical companies increasingly depend on for consistent, cost-effective ingredient supply.
Where Individual Manufacturers Fit Into This Larger Story
Within this broader industry evolution, individual manufacturers have carved out their own specific niches, often built around particular therapeutic categories, specialized manufacturing capabilities, or long-standing relationships with specific client segments. A company’s history within this timeline, how long it has operated, which certifications it pursued early versus later, and how it responded to industry-wide shifts, often says a great deal about its operational philosophy and adaptability.
Manufacturers that entered the export certification race early frequently built stronger, more entrenched client relationships simply by virtue of being among the first reliable options available to international formulators during a period when trusted domestic suppliers were still relatively scarce.
Workforce And Technical Expertise As An Underappreciated Asset
Pharmaceutical manufacturing, despite being capital-intensive, ultimately depends heavily on skilled technical personnel capable of managing complex chemical processes, quality systems, and regulatory documentation. Companies that have invested consistently in workforce training and retention over the years often develop institutional knowledge that becomes difficult for newer entrants to replicate quickly, creating a form of competitive advantage that doesn’t always show up clearly in financial statements but matters considerably for long-term operational reliability.
This accumulated expertise, built through years of navigating regulatory inspections, process optimizations, and evolving compliance requirements, often represents one of the more durable, if less visible, assets a pharmaceutical manufacturer carries into its public market journey.
Understanding What Happens After Bidding Concludes
For investors participating in any public offering, the period immediately following the bidding window brings its own set of considerations, particularly around how shares get distributed across applicant categories. Checking
ipo allotment status
typically becomes the primary point of reference during this window, helping applicants understand allocation outcomes before shares are credited to their accounts ahead of listing.
Considering The Road Ahead For Established Manufacturers
Looking forward, pharmaceutical manufacturers with established histories face a somewhat different set of questions compared to newer entrants, centered less around building initial credibility and more around sustaining relevance amid evolving therapeutic demand, tightening environmental regulations, and continuous pressure to modernize manufacturing processes without disrupting existing client relationships built over years of consistent supply.
Points Worth Reflecting On Before Forming A View
How long the company has operated within India’s evolving pharmaceutical manufacturing landscape
Timing and breadth of its international regulatory certifications
Workforce stability and technical expertise retention over time
Adaptability demonstrated through past industry shifts or regulatory changes
Strategic priorities articulated for the business going forward as a listed entity
Looking at a pharmaceutical manufacturer through this historical and structural lens offers a different, arguably more grounded, way of understanding its position, one that goes beyond a single year’s financial snapshot to capture how decades of industry evolution have shaped the business standing for public investment today.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration plans to use a
new approach to deny Medicaid coverage
of drugs for gender-affirming care. The precedent it sets could be used to avoid paying for other drugs, too, upending an expectation that Medicaid covers the vast majority of prescription medication.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
issued a final rule
this month barring the use of federal Medicaid and CHIP funding to pay for pediatric gender-affirming medications and surgery. The rule, set to go into effect Oct. 13, attracted attention because it’s the latest development in the administration’s campaign to halt transgender health care for young people.
Advertisement
But Medicaid experts say the rule could set a precedent for denying coverage of drugs and other services beyond gender-affirming care. In general, Medicaid must cover most outpatient drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration for medically accepted indications, as long as drug companies agree to pay significant rebates to Medicaid to be part of the program.

Pharma Associations.url_match_title: K-Bio Licensing Deals Top $12 Billion, Near Record High - Businesskorea
Pharma Associations.content:
Major Deals With Global Drugmakers Fuel Surge in Overseas Licensing
The Korea Pharmaceutical and Bio-Pharma Manufacturers Association building in Seoul.
South Korea's pharmaceutical and biotech industry is on track to set a new annual record for overseas licensing deals, with the cumulative value of deals signed by domestic companies this year surpassing 17 trillion won. According to the Korea Pharmaceutical and Bio-Pharma Manufacturers Association, the cumulative value of the deals stood at approximately 17.25 trillion won, or about $12.46 billion, based on 12 deals excluding undisclosed agreements.
Hanmi Pharmaceutical said on Aug. 24 that it had signed a licensing agreement with Genentech, a subsidiary of global pharmaceutical giant Roche, for its obesity drug candidate HM17321. The deal is worth up to $2.3 billion with Hanmi Pharmaceutical receiving an upfront payment of $190 million. The agreement is considered the largest single-candidate licensing deal in the history of South Korea's pharmaceutical industry.
HM17321, the licensed drug candidate, is based on urocortin 2, or UCN2, and is designed to promote weight loss while preserving muscle mass. It uses a mechanism distinct from existing GLP-1 therapies and is considered a key pipeline in Hanmi Pharmaceutical's H.O.P. project for obesity and metabolic diseases. Earlier this year, Hanmi Pharmaceutical also licensed its novel drug candidate for obesity, sonefpeglutide, to Eli Lilly in a deal worth up to $1.19 billion.
South Korean biotech startups have also been stepping up their licensing activity. Alteogen signed a deal earlier this month worth up to $365 million with a global pharmaceutical company for the development of a subcutaneous formulation using its Hybrozyme platform technology, ALT-B4. NeoImmuneTech also signed an agreement with U.S.-based Tolerance Bio to transfer exclusive rights to its T-cell amplifier NT-I7, in a deal that could provide up to $260 million in milestone payments.
The results are seen as being underpinned by aggressive research and development spending by South Korean companies. The five largest domestic pharmaceutical companies, including Yuhan Corp., Chong Kun Dang and Hanmi Pharmaceutical, spent a combined 562.8 billion won on R&D in the first half, up 16% from a year earlier. Major biotech companies such as Celltrion and SK Biopharmaceuticals also invested 284.3 billion won and 97.3 billion won, respectively, in R&D during the first half, strengthening their technological competitiveness.
The expansion of licensing activity beyond the industry's traditional focus on cancer treatments to areas such as obesity, Alzheimer's disease and autoimmune disorders is also viewed positively. An industry official said global interest in K-Bio has grown as accumulated R&D investments have translated into concrete clinical data. If the current trend continues, the industry broadly expects this year's licensing deals to surpass last year's annual record.
Choi Mun-hee

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: GSK (LSE/NYSE: GSK) Stock Slips Despite FDA Priority Review And Japan Approval Across Two Key Drug Programs - foreignpolicyjournal.com
Regulatory Agencies.content:
GSK plc (LSE/NYSE: GSK) shares edged lower in early Monday trading, even as the pharmaceutical company announced two significant regulatory developments across its oncology and hepatology pipelines.
The US Food and Drug Administration accepted for priority review a supplemental Biologics License Application for Jemperli (dostarlimab) in previously untreated stage II and III dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer.
The FDA has set a PDUFA action date of February 2027 for the application, which was submitted under the agency’s Project Orbis scheme for coordinated international review.
The submission is also eligible for expedited assessment through the National Priority Voucher programme, adding another potential pathway to accelerate the drug’s regulatory journey.
Data backing the application came from the phase II AZUR-1 trial, which enrolled 154 participants and showed a meaningful proportion remained free of detectable cancer a year or more after treatment.
If approved, Jemperli could become the first immunotherapy capable of sparing certain rectal cancer patients from chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, representing a significant shift in treatment standards.
On a separate front, GSK secured its first global approval for Hibsago (bepirovirsen), after Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare cleared the antisense oligonucleotide as a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B.
The Japanese approval, accelerated through the country’s SENKU designation, applies to adults who have completed at least six months of prior nucleoside analogue therapy.
Phase III B-Well data underpinning the Hibsago approval demonstrated a 19% functional cure rate compared to roughly 1% for standard care alone, a result GSK’s Chief Scientific Officer Tony Wood described as “a major advance” for hepatitis B management.
GSK said US and other regulatory decisions on Hibsago are expected in the coming months, potentially opening the drug to a far larger global patient population.
Despite positive momentum across two therapeutic areas and progress on multiple regulatory fronts, investors responded with caution, with GSK shares trading marginally lower on the day of the announcements.
The muted market reaction suggests investors may be adopting a wait-and-see approach ahead of the February 2027 PDUFA date for Jemperli and the anticipated international regulatory verdicts for Hibsago.

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: Op-Ed: How The FDA’s Green List For GLP-1 Drugs Fuels The Gray Market Problem - AOL.com
Regulatory Agencies.content:
The FDA’s recent inclusion of certain GLP-1 receptor agonists on a so-called “Green List” is often portrayed as a regulatory milestone aimed at ensuring safer access to these increasingly popular medications. However, beneath the surface, this policy move may ironically serve to legitimize and even entrench a burgeoning gray market around GLP-1 drugs, with profound implications for patient safety, healthcare equity, and pharmaceutical regulation.
GLP-1 receptor agonists—originally designed to treat type 2 diabetes—have gained explosive popularity off-label, especially for weight management and metabolic health. This surging demand has outpaced formal channels of prescription and distribution, spawning widespread direct-to-consumer sales through unofficial websites, compounding pharmacies, and global online suppliers. Many patients seeking these medications face long waits, insurance denials, or high out-of-pocket costs, driving them toward these gray markets.
By creating a Green List that acknowledges certain GLP-1 products as “allowed” or “preferred,” the FDA ostensibly wants to direct patients and healthcare providers toward safer, vetted versions. Yet this approach has a major policy paradox: it simultaneously draws a tacit boundary between “approved” and “non-approved” products without substantially tightening enforcement against gray market purveyors. The list may inadvertently signal to consumers that purchasing from these green-listed sources is “acceptable,” while failing to diminish demand for unlisted or counterfeit alternatives, which often flourish in parallel.
Critically, this policy falls short of addressing the root drivers of the gray market. The FDA’s approach seems premised on the assumption that supply-side regulation—vetting which GLP-1 formulations can circulate—will curtail unsafe use. But the persistence of structural barriers—high costs, insurance hurdles, limited prescribing capacity—ensures ongoing gaps between demand and legitimate supply. As long as these systemic challenges remain unaddressed, the gray market will continue to thrive under a new guise of partial legitimacy.
Moreover, this FDA tactic risks creating a two-tiered system of access: patients with means or knowledge to navigate the Green List and secure recommended products, and others left vulnerable to unregulated, potentially unsafe alternatives. Rather than eliminate uncertainty, the policy may amplify confusion about product legitimacy and quality, undermining public trust.
Advertisement
The move also reveals a cautious regulatory posture that appears reactive rather than proactive. Instead of aggressively expanding legitimate access channels—such as through faster approvals for generics or innovative payment models—the FDA’s Green List acts as a stopgap, implicitly accepting gray market realities rather than confronting them head-on with comprehensive reforms.
In sum, while the FDA’s Green List for GLP-1 drugs aims to guide safer medication use, its limited scope and ambivalent enforcement risk reinforcing the very gray market it seeks to constrain. A more effective policy would integrate robust demand-side solutions, enhanced patient education, and stronger cross-border regulatory cooperation to ultimately dismantle unsafe supply chains rather than merely “legitimize” portions of the gray area. Without such broader reforms, the Green List may become a regulatory band-aid on an increasingly complex pharmaceutical access crisis.

Regulatory Agencies.url_match_title: Early Detection of Alzheimer's with a Drop of Blood... Consecutive FDA Approvals in the U.S. - 아시아경제
Regulatory Agencies.content:
Roche and Eli Lilly's Jointly Developed 'Tau' Test
FDA Grants Approval; Fourth Test Cleared in Two Years
More than 4,500 Devices in Use—Major Advantage in Accessibility
In the United States, simple blood tests for the early detection of Alzheimer's disease are increasingly clearing regulatory hurdles. Since the first approval in May of last year, the fourth Alzheimer's blood test has already received regulatory approval, raising expectations that patients may soon face less of a burden.
View original image
According to U.S. political outlet The Hill and other foreign media on August 24 (local time), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the 'Elecsys Phospho-Tau 217 (pTau217)' blood test co-developed by global pharmaceutical companies Roche and Eli Lilly. This test measures phosphorylated tau 217 in the blood of patients aged 55 or older with cognitive impairment, helping doctors assess whether Alzheimer's-related amyloid pathology may be present in the brain.
Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche. Photo by Reuters Yonhap News.
View original image
According to Roche, this test is the first and only FDA-approved blood test that helps confirm or rule out amyloid pathology using a single biomarker. However, it is not a standalone diagnostic for Alzheimer's; results must be interpreted alongside other clinical information.
The greatest strength of this test is its accessibility. It can be used on more than 4,500 Roche testing devices already installed across the United States, and major diagnostic companies LabCorp and Quest Diagnostics also plan to offer the service through their laboratory networks. However, Roche has not disclosed the price of the test.
This marks the fourth time since May of last year that an Alzheimer's blood test has received FDA approval in the United States. Previously, Fujirebio’s ‘Lumipulse’ was authorized as the first blood-based test to aid in Alzheimer’s diagnosis.
Traditionally, checking for amyloid buildup in the brain associated with Alzheimer’s has required either positron emission tomography (PET) or cerebrospinal fluid analysis. However, PET has limitations due to costs and equipment accessibility. Cerebrospinal fluid tests also caused considerable discomfort, as they involve inserting a needle into the lower back to collect fluid.
With the advent of new treatments that can slow the progression of Alzheimer’s, there is an increasing need to identify early-stage patients—those who stand to benefit from these therapies—more quickly. As a result, pharmaceutical and diagnostic companies are accelerating the race to develop more convenient blood-based tests.

The regulatory landscape across life sciences has faced unprecedented shifts over the past year. Simultaneous realignments of FDA, EU, and ISO frameworks have converged, demanding unified compliance strategies that satisfy global standards. Compounding this challenge, regulatory bodies have heightened their oversight capabilities by leveraging enhanced speed, deeper access, and advanced inspection methods. For organisations doing business in regulated environments, this intense scrutiny demands an immediate transition from traditional, periodic readiness toward achieving a continual state of compliance.
